## **Preface**

The purpose of this book is to show how algebraic geometry methods can be used to solve different problems in the fields of robotics and control theory, including in the last topic both analysis of dynamic systems and control design.

It is perhaps reductive to see the link between such disciplines based on the fact that algebraic geometry provides algorithms to solve, mostly in an exact manner and often parameterizing sets of solutions, systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities, which are very useful for the design of control laws and observers; as it will be seen throughout the book, algebraic geometry also provides the notions and concepts, such as ideals and varieties, to properly formalize some of the problems under study.

The various applications presented in this book are naturally originated from our previous research experience, and certainly do not exhaust the richness of results that can be obtained in robotics and control theory by using the techniques typical of algebraic geometry; with this in mind, just to help the reader willing to use the same methodologies, we have tried to detail as much as possible our derivations, illustrating with small examples also some of the relatively easy steps, with the purpose of being as much introductory as possible. In some cases, the examples are very simple: this is done on purpose to better emphasize the meaning of the concepts, together with the algorithmic aspects.

It is not assumed that the reader already knows algebraic geometry, only some basic knowledge of calculus and linear algebra is  required; therefore, Chapter 1 is devoted to a concise but rigorous exposition of all the basic notions needed in this book; an effort has been made to render the description self contained and to illustrate every concept by examples, most of which simple enough so that computations can be performed by hand. However, such a first chapter is not aimed at a thorough presentation of the topic, so that proofs and also many results that do not find application here are not reported; for a deeper understanding of algebraic geometry the reader is referred to the cited texts, especially Cox *et al.* (2015).

To further guide the reader to effectively use the proposed methodologies and algorithms, in Chapter it is illustrated how the computations referred to in the examples of Chapter 1 can be performed on `Macaulay2`, a free CAS (computer algebra system). It is worth stressing that most of the computations described in the book can be performed by other CAS, `Macaulay2`has been preferred because it is free and complete as for the functionalities needed here.

After the first two chapters, the order of exposition is mostly based on the rationale of postponing further developments of the theory until the chapter or section in which they are used, this means that specifications of the general concepts exposed in Chapter 1 can be found in subsequent sections, just at the point in which they are needed.

As for robotics and control theory, it is assumed that the reader knows the fundamentals of dynamic systems theory and some standard tools in control design, such as Lyapunov stability basic theorems and, as for linear systems, structural properties and observer design principles; however, the problems have been mostly formulated in a self-contained manner, and, only in some cases where to recall more background would have been distracting, references are given to books or papers where the required concepts are introduced. Apart from such references, which are needed to complete or deepen what reported in the book, and others that are at some point necessary to better define our approach, we did not systematically include survey sections in the different chapters; this is due to the number and heterogeneity of the applications considered, it would have been very difficult to obtain a reasonably complete overview on each of the topics touched. We apologize for such an omission and we hope that the references included sufficiently complete this aspect.

## **About the Authors**

![image](images/aut1.jpg)

**Laura Menini** received the Laurea degree in 1993 and the Ph.D. in 1997, from the University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy, where she is currently Full Professor. She co-authored the books *Symmetries and Semi-invariants in the Analysis of Nonlinear Systems* (Springer, 2011) and *Mathematical Methods for System Theory* (World Scientific, 1998). She is Chair of the IFAC Coordinating Committee 2 — Design Method and Senior Editor of the IEEE Control Systems Letters.

![image](images/aut2.jpg)

**Corrado Possieri** received his Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Medical Engineering and his Ph.D. degree in Computer Science, Control and Geoinformation from the University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy, in 2011, 2013, and 2016, respectively. In 2016, he visited the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB). In 2018, he joined the Department of Electronics and Telecommunications at Politecnico di Torino, where he was an Assistant Professor. Subsequently, in 2019, he joined the Institute for Systems Analysis and Computer Science of the National Research Council of Italy (IASI-CNR), where he is currently a Researcher. He is Associate  Editor of IEEE CSS Conference Editorial Board, of the EUCA Conference Editorial Board, and of the IFAC Conference Editorial Board.

![image](images/aut3.jpg)

**Antonio Tornambè** is currently Full Professor of Control Theory at University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy. His research interests include control theory for linear and nonlinear systems. He is the co-author of *Discrete-Event System Theory: An Introduction* (World Scientific, 1995), *Mathematical Methods for System Theory* (World Scientific, 1998), and *Symmetries and Semi-invariants in the Analysis of Nonlinear Systems* (Springer, 2011).

## **Chapter 1**

## **Algebraic Geometry Notions**

### **1.1 Affine varieties and polynomial ideals**

A *monomial* in the single *variables x*[1], . . . , *x[n]* is a product of the form

![image](images/eq1-1.jpg)

where the *α[i]*’s are non-negative integers. Let *x* denote *x* = \[*x*[1] . . . *x[n]*\]^⊤. To shorten the notation, the product in (1.1) is also written as *x^α*, where *α* = (*α*[1], . . . , *α[n]*) is the ordered tuple (referred to as *multi–index*) of the exponents in the monomial. The *total degree* of *x^α*, denoted |*α*|, is defined as the sum of the exponents, i.e., |*α*| := *α*[1] + · · · + *α[n]*. In the following, any tuple is considered ordered.

Let ![image](images/kopf.jpg)be a *field*, such as, e.g., ![image](images/qopf.jpg), ![image](images/ropf.jpg)or ![image](images/copf.jpg), i.e., the set of rational, real or complex numbers, respectively. Whenever a problem is to be recast in an algebraic geometry setting, it is needed to specify at the very beginning which is the field used for the analysis. Such a field is referred to as *ambient field*. When a change of ambient field is necessary for some of the steps of the problem solution, this is specified and, if convenient, emphasized with appropriate notation. Let ![image](images/zopf.jpg)be the set of integers. Given *m* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg), the symbol ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)*m*] denotes the set of integers greater than or equal to *m*. Similarly, given *r* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg), the symbol ![image](images/ropf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)*r*] denotes the set of real numbers greater than or equal to *r*.

A *polynomial p* in *x*, with coefficients in the field ![image](images/kopf.jpg), is a finite ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\-linear combination of monomials and is written as follows:

![image](images/eq1-2.jpg)

where ![image](images/capa.jpg)is a finite set (without repetitions) of tuples *α* = (*α*[1], . . . , *α[n]*), with *α[i]* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0], *i* = 1, . . . , *n*; if all coefficients *a[α]*, *α* ∈ ![image](images/capa.jpg), are zero, the corresponding polynomial is referred to as the *zero polynomial*. A product of a non-zero element in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)and a monomial appearing in a polynomial (i.e., one of the *a[α]x^α*’s appearing in (1.2), with *a[α]* ≠ 0) is referred to as a *term* of the polynomial. The *total degree* deg(*p*) of a polynomial *p* is the maximum of the total degrees of the monomials appearing in its terms (it is pointed out that all terms *a[α]x^α* in *p* have a non-zero coefficient *a[α]*). The total degree of the zero polynomial is not defined, because the set of the terms of the zero polynomial is empty. For a polynomial *p* in a single variable, the total degree coincides with the usual degree of *p*.

Let ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\] (or, briefly, ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]) be the ring of all polynomials in *x*[1], . . . , *x[n]* with coefficients in the ambient field ![image](images/kopf.jpg); when working with polynomials in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], the ring ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] is called the *ambient ring*. Note that it is preferable to specify which is the ambient ring, because, whereas it seems natural to consider the polynomial

![image](images/eq1-3.jpg)

in the ambient ring ![image](images/qopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[3]\], for the polynomial

![image](images/eq1-4.jpg)

it is not so obvious if it has to be considered in the ambient ring ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[3]\] or in ![image](images/qopf.jpg)(![image](images/root2.jpg))\[*x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[3]\], where ![image](images/qopf.jpg)(![image](images/root2.jpg)) is the smallest finite algebraic extension of ![image](images/qopf.jpg)containing ![image](images/root2.jpg).

A *rational function* in *x* with coefficients in the field ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is a quotient ![image](images/pbyq.jpg), where *p* and *q* are polynomials in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] and *q* is different from the zero polynomial. Two rational functions ![image](images/i0002-01.jpg)and ![image](images/i0002-02.jpg)are equal if *p[a]q[b]*−*p[b]q[a]* is the zero polynomial in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]. It is worth pointing out that the set of the rational functions in *x* with coefficients in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)has the mathematical structure of a field and is denoted, in the following, through the symbols ![image](images/kopf.jpg)(*x*) and frac(![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]).

Given a field ![image](images/kopf.jpg)and a positive integer *n*, define the *n-dimensional affine space* over ![image](images/kopf.jpg)as

![image](images/f0003-01.jpg)

Polynomials can easily be related to affine spaces. The key idea is that any polynomial *p* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] yields a polynomial function (denoted with the same symbol)

![image](images/f0003-02.jpg)

which associates to any *x̂* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^n* a unique *p*(*x̂*), which is obtained through the substitution *x* = *x̂* in the polynomial *p*. Note that if ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is not finite as a field (as, for instance, ![image](images/qopf.jpg), ![image](images/ropf.jpg)or ![image](images/copf.jpg)), then *p* is the zero polynomial in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] if and only if the corresponding polynomial function *p* : ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^n* → ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is zero, *p*(*x̂*) = 0, for all *x̂* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg). On the other hand, if ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is a finite field (i.e., a field constituted by a finite number of elements), there may be non-zero polynomials *p* in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] such that the corresponding polynomial function *p* : ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^n* → ![image](images/kopf.jpg)satisfies *p*(*x̂*) = 0, ∀*x̂* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg), as shown in the following example.

**Example 1.1.1.** Let {0, 1} be a set endowed with the structure of a field by defining the sum and product operations as follows:

![image](images/f0003-03.jpg)

where 0 and 1 are the additive and multiplicative identities, respectively. This is a finite field (actually, the smallest one), which is denoted ![image](images/fopf.jpg)[2] in the following. Consider the polynomial

![image](images/f0003-04.jpg)

where *z* is a single variable, which vanishes at *z* = 0 and *z* = 1: this is a non-zero polynomial yielding the zero function on ![image](images/fopf.jpg)[2].

Different ambient rings constitute different mathematical entities. Hence, given *p*[1](*x*) = *x* in ![image](images/qopf.jpg)\[*x*\] and *p*[2](*x, y*) = 3*x* + ![image](images/root2.jpg)*y* in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*x, y*\], where *x* and *y* are single variables, it makes no sense to define the sum *p*[1] + *p*[2]. However, each polynomial in ![image](images/qopf.jpg)\[*x*\] can also be thought of as a polynomial in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*x, y*\] and, therefore, with the *coercion* of *p*[1] in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*x, y*\], the sum *p*[1] +*p*[2] makes sense. Thus, coercion is a fundamental  tool that can be used when working with polynomials belonging to different rings.

The coercion can operate at different levels; in particular, if ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1] and ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2] are two fields such that ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1] ⊆ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2], any element in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1]\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\] can be coerced into ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2]\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\], or, considering the additional single variables *y*[1], . . . , *y[m]*, any element in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1]\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\] can be coerced into either ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1]\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n], y*[1], . . . , *y[m]*\] or ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2]\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n], y*[1], . . . , *y[m]*\].

The field ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is said to be *algebraically closed* if any non-constant polynomial in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*z*\], where *z* is a single variable, has a root in ![image](images/kopf.jpg). For instance, ![image](images/ropf.jpg)is not algebraically closed because the roots of *z*² + 1 are not in ![image](images/ropf.jpg), whereas ![image](images/copf.jpg)is algebraically closed because, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (Cox *et al.*, 2015, Theorem 7 at page 4), any polynomial in ![image](images/copf.jpg)\[*z*\] has a root in ![image](images/copf.jpg).

If ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is a field and *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* are polynomials in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], the set

![image](images/f0004-01.jpg)

is called the *affine variety* in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^n* defined by *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*, and ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^n* is called the *corresponding affine space*. To avoid confusion, if ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1] and ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2] are two fields such that ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1] ⊆ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2], given *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1]\[*x*\], the symbol **V**[![image](images/subkopf.jpg)[2]](*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*) can be used to denote the set

![image](images/f0004-02.jpg)

In the following, to avoid confusion, given two fields ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1] and ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2], ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1] ⊆ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2], and given *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1]\[*x*\], the symbol 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉[![image](images/subkopf.jpg)2\[*x,y*\]] denotes the ideal in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2]\[*x, y*\], generated by *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* coerced into ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2]\[*x, y*\], where *y* = \[*y*[1] . . . *y[m]*\]^⊤ is a vector of some additional single variables; ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[2] may coincide with ![image](images/kopf.jpg)[1], and *y* can be missing.

An ideal that can be generated by one polynomial is referred to as a *principal* ideal. Non-zero polynomial ideals in a single variable are always principal.

A nice interpretation of ideals can be given in terms of polynomial equations. Given *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], consider the polynomial system (1.5), from which new equations can be generated. which is a “consequence” of system (1.5) (i.e., if (1.5) holds with *x* = *x̂*, for some *x̂* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^n*, then (1.6) holds for the same *x* = *x̂*). Hence, since the polynomial on the left-hand side of (1.6) belongs to 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉 and any other element of 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉 can be obtained as the left-hand side of (1.6) for some choice of *c*[1], . . . *c[s]*, the ideal 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉  consists of all “polynomial consequences” of system (1.5), i.e., it is the set of all new polynomial equations that can be obtained from (1.5) by *elementary operations*, i.e., products by scalar polynomials and sums.

It is worth mentioning that the same ideal can have different minimal bases, even with a different number of elements; for instance, {*z*} and {*z* + *z*³, *z*²} are two minimal bases of the same ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*z*\], where *z* is single variable. To improve intuition, there is a nice analogy between ideals and subspaces: both are closed under sum and multiplication, except that for vector spaces one multiplies by scalars in a field, whereas for ideals one multiplies by scalars (actually, scalar polynomials) in a ring.

Given *p* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\], it may be convenient to fix the values of some entries of *x*; for instance, if the values of the first *m* < *n* entries of *x* are fixed, *x[i]* = *x̂[i]*, with *x̂[i]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg), *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, then the resulting *p*(*x̂*[1], . . . , *x̂[m], x*[*m*+1], . . . , *x[n]*) can be coerced into ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*[*m*+1], . . . , *x[n]*\]. Similarly, ideals can also be specialized; for instance, if ![image](images/capi.jpg)\= 〈*p*[1](*β, x*), . . . , *p[s]*(*β, x*)〉 is an ideal in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*β, x*\], then ![image](images/capi.jpg)*[![image](images/subbetacirc.jpg)]* = 〈*p*[1](*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*, *x*), . . . , *p[s]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*, *x*)〉, with the entries of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)* in ![image](images/kopf.jpg), can be thought of as an ideal in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\].

In [Section 1.1](#chapter1.xhtml#sec1-1), the basic notions of commutative algebra on polynomial rings and of geometry of affine varieties have been introduced and the connections between them have been highlighted. In this section, the basic notions of computational algebraic geometry, which allow one to solve problems about ideals in an algorithmic fashion, are recalled.

There are three kinds of *elementary operations* that can be carried out on the rows of a matrix *M* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*n*):

(i) Interchange two rows.

(ii) Multiply a row by a non-zero scalar in ![image](images/kopf.jpg).

(iii) Add to a row any other row multiplied by a scalar in ![image](images/kopf.jpg).

A *row echelon form* ![image](images/cape.jpg)(*M*) of a matrix *M* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*n*), which can always be obtained by a finite sequence of elementary operations on the rows of *M*, satisfies:

(a) All non-zero rows of ![image](images/cape.jpg)(*M*) precede all its zero rows.

(b) The first non-zero entry in a non-zero row of ![image](images/cape.jpg)(*M*) (which is called the *leading coefficient* of the row, or *pivot*) appears to the right of the first non-zero entry in the preceding row.

(c) The leading coefficients of ![image](images/cape.jpg)(*M*) are all equal to 1.

If, in addition to the above properties (a)–(c), one has that

(d) the leading coefficient is the only non-zero entry in its column,

such a row echelon form of *M* is said to be *reduced* and is denoted ![image](images/cape.jpg)*[r]*(*M*); ![image](images/cape.jpg)*[r]*(*M*) can always be obtained by a finite sequence of elementary operations on the rows of *M*. Unlike a row echelon form, the reduced row echelon form is uniquely determined, because it does not depend on the sequence of elementary operations used for its computation.

A row echelon form and the reduced row echelon form of a matrix *M* can be computed through the Gauss and Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithms (Meyer, 2000), respectively. The Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithm is reported in the following, where the symbol \[*M*\]*[k,j]* is used to denote the (*k, j*)th entry of *M*.

The main goal of the remainder of this section and of the following sections is to extend the univariate polynomial division algorithm and the elimination features of the Gauss–Jordan algorithm to the case of multivariate polynomials. Analyzing the univariate polynomial division and the Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithms, one can observe that the notion of order is a key topic of both these algorithms. In fact, to perform the division algorithm between two univariate polynomials, one is implicitly using the degree order on the single variable monomials,

![image](images/f0020-02.jpg)

where *z* is a single variable, whereas, to perform the Gauss–Jordan elimination algorithm, one is implicitly using the following order of the single variables:

![image](images/f0020-03.jpg)

Clearly, to consider multivariate polynomials, one has to combine both the above orders somehow.

A possible approach to extend the above orders to multivariate polynomials is to introduce the notion of monomial order, i.e., an order on the terms of the polynomials belonging to ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\]. First, note that each monomial ![image](images/i0020-01.jpg)is uniquely determined by the tuple of exponents *α* = (*α*[1], . . . , *α[n]*), and *vice versa*. Therefore, any order ≻ established on the tuples *α* gives an order on the monomials *x^α*. With this equivalence in mind, a *monomial order* on ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], denoted ≻, is a relation on the set of monomials *x^α* such that:

(i) ≻ is a *total order*, i.e., for each pair *x^α*, *x^γ*, either *x^α* ≻ *x^γ*, or *x^α* = *x^γ* or *x^α* ≺ *x^γ*;

(ii) given *x^α*, *x^γ* such that *x^α* ≻ *x^γ* and a multi-index *δ*, one has that *x*^(*α*+*δ*) ≻ *x*^(*γ*+*δ*);

(iii) ≻ is a *well* order, i.e., each non-empty set of monomials has a smallest element.

Two important examples of monomial orders are the *lexicographic order* (briefly, Lex monomial order), denoted ≻[Lex], and the *graded reverse lexicographic order* (briefly, GRL monomial order), denoted ≻[GRL]. Let *α, γ* ∈ ![image](images/i0021-01.jpg)be given. One has that *α* ≻[Lex] *γ* (or, equivalently, *x^α* ≻[Lex] *x^γ*, with *x*[1] ≻[Lex] . . . ≻[Lex] *x[n]*), if the first nonzero entry of the vector difference *α* − *γ* is positive. On the other hand, one has that *α* ≻[GRL] *γ* (or, equivalently, *x^α* ≻[GRL] *x^γ*, with *x*[1] ≻[GRL] . . . ≻[GRL] *x[n]*), if |*α*| > |*γ*|, or |*α*| = |*γ*| and the last non-zero entry of *α* − *γ* is negative. Clearly, these two orders may arrange the monomials in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] in different ways.

Using the convention 〈![image](images/0sl.jpg)〉 = {0}, the empty set ![image](images/0sl.jpg)is thought of as the Gröbner basis of the zero ideal {0}. With this convention, it turns out that any ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] admits a (not necessarily unique) Gröbner basis and any Gröbner basis of an ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)is actually a basis of ![image](images/capi.jpg)(Buchberger, 2006). A Gröbner basis ![image](images/capg.jpg)\= {*g*[1], . . . , *g[m]*} is said to be *reduced* if LC(*g[i]*) = 1, *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, and *g[i]* is reduced with respect to (*g*[1], . . . , *g*[*i*−1], *g*[*i*+1], . . . , *g[m]*) (i.e., no monomial of *g[i]* lies in 〈LT(![image](images/capg.jpg)\\ {*g[i]*})〉). Any ideal has a unique reduced Gröbner basis with respect to the chosen monomial order.

Note that the coefficients of the polynomials in a Gröbner basis ![image](images/capg.jpg)of an ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)in ![image](images/qopf.jpg)\[*x*\] are ratios of, often big, elements of ![image](images/zopf.jpg)(similarly, when ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\= ![image](images/qopf.jpg)(*β*), for some vector *β* of parameters); if convenient, to simplify the expressions of such polynomials, all denominators are cleared, without explicit mention, from which the condition LC(*g[i]*) = 1, *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, need not hold in the reported examples of reduced Gröbner bases.

An interesting property of Gröbner bases is that, once any monomial order has been chosen on ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], although a Gröbner basis ![image](images/capg.jpg)of an ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] is not unique, for any polynomial *p* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], the remainder of the division of *p* by ![image](images/capg.jpg)is unique; to point out the independence from ![image](images/capg.jpg)of the remainder of the division of *p* by ![image](images/capg.jpg), such a remainder is denoted *p*%![image](images/capi.jpg)and called the *normal form* of *p* by ![image](images/capi.jpg). In addition, if *p*%![image](images/capi.jpg)\= 0 for some monomial order, then it is zero for any other monomial order. Hence, the use of Gröbner bases completely solves the ideal membership problem, because *p* ∈ ![image](images/capi.jpg)if and only if *p*%![image](images/capi.jpg)\= 0 for some monomial order.

An algorithm to compute a Gröbner basis ![image](images/capg.jpg)of a given ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)is given in Cox *et al.* (2015, Theorem 2 at page 91) and is summarized in [Algorithm 1.2.4](#chapter1.xhtml#alg1-2-4).

Algorithm 1.2.4: The Buchberger algorithm.

![image](images/alg1-2-4.jpg)

**Remark 1.2.1.** Some comments about such an algorithm are given to allow the reader to better understand [Algorithm 1.2.4](#chapter1.xhtml#alg1-2-4). The polynomial *s* defined at Step 7 is called the S*\-polynomial* of *p* and *q*, denoted S(*p, q*). It is worth mentioning that such a polynomial is in the ideal 〈*p, q*〉 and that it is specifically designed to produce the cancellation of the leading terms of *p* and *q*. In Buchberger (2006), it has been proved that ![image](images/capg.jpg)\= {*g*[1], . . . , *g[r]*} is a Gröbner basis of the ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)if and only if, for all pairs *i* ≠ *j*, the remainder of the division of S(*g[i], g[j]*) by the elements of ![image](images/capg.jpg)(listed in arbitrary order) is zero (this fact is usually known as the *Buchberger criterion*). Hence, the algorithm terminates at Step 13 providing a Gröbner basis of the ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)\= 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉. However, such a basis is not in general reduced, because the generators *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* of the ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)are always contained in a basis thus obtained. In fact, the algorithm extends the basis {*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*} by successively appending non-zero remainders of the division of S(*g[i], g[j]*) by (*g*[1], . . . , *g[r]*). This iterative extension of the ideal basis suggests the complexity underlying the computation of Gröbner bases. In fact, it has been proved (Bardet, 2005) that the computation of Gröbner bases is an EXPSPACE-complete problem. However, as shown in Lazard (1983), the running time and storage space required for the computation of a Gröbner basis seem to be manageable “on average” by a modern computer, making it possible to efficiently apply such tools.

### **1.3 Homogeneous polynomials and ideals**

A polynomial *p* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] is *homogeneous* of total degree *d* (it is referred to as a *form* of total degree *d*) if each monomial in *p* has total degree *d*. Given *p* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], let *p[d]* be the sum of all terms of *p* of total degree *d*; each *p[d]* is homogeneous, *p* = ∑*[d] p[d]*, and the *p[d]*’s are called the *homogeneous components* of *p*.

**Definition 1.3.1.** An ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] is *homogeneous* if for any *p* ∈ ![image](images/capi.jpg), the homogeneous components of *p* are in ![image](images/capi.jpg)as well.

### **1.4 Elimination theory**

In this section, the basic notions of the elimination theory are briefly recalled, describing the process of elimination of variables from a system of polynomial equations. Such a process extends the Gauss–Jordan algorithm to nonlinear systems of polynomial equations and is of great help in the subsequent development of control theory applications.

The polynomials *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] are *linearly dependent* if there are *m* scalars *c*[1], . . . , *c[m]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg), not all zero, such that *c*[1]*p*[1] +. . . +*c[m]p[s]* is the zero polynomial in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] (*linearly independent*, otherwise). The polynomials *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] are *algebraically dependent* if there is a non-zero polynomial *q* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*y*[1], . . . , *y[m]*\] such that *q*(*p*[1](*x*), . . . , *p[s]*(*x*)) is the zero polynomial in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] (*algebraically independent*, otherwise). Clearly, linear dependence implies algebraic dependence (if *c*[1]*p*[1] + · · · + *c[m]p[s]* = 0, then one can take *q*(*y*[1], . . . , *y[s]*) = *c*[1]*y*[1] + · · · + *c[s]y[s]*), whereas algebraic independence implies linear independence.

The main geometric interpretation of [Theorem 1.4.1](#chapter1.xhtml#the1-4-1) is that the elimination of variables in an ideal is similar to the projection of the corresponding affine variety onto a lower dimensional subspace. Hence, if one is interested in solutions of a system of polynomial equations only in some of the unknowns, elimination theory provides an efficient tool to obtain them.

The following example shows how elimination of variables is effective in case of linear systems, using determinant theory.

#### **1.4.1 *Resultants***

So far, the elimination theory has been presented from the point of view of Gröbner bases. The exposition of the elimination theory is concluded introducing the resultant of two polynomials in a single variable and pointing out its connection with the Gröbner bases.

A nice property of the resultant Res(*p, q, z*) is that it is a polynomial in the coefficients of *p* and *q*. Furthermore, *p* and *q* have a common factor in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*z*\] if and only if Res(*p, q, z*) = 0. To link resultants to elimination, consider the following theorem.

### **1.7 Root localization**

Before tackling the problem of root localization, some notions are recalled about symmetric matrices and quadratic forms.

Let *Q* be a symmetric square matrix in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*), and let *q*(*ξ*) = *ξ*^⊤*Qξ* be the associated quadratic form, where *ξ* = \[*ξ*[1] . . . *ξ[m]*\]^⊤. Any non-singular matrix *V* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*) transforms *Q* into another symmetric matrix *Q̌* = *V*^⊤*QV* in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*); matrices *Q* and *Q̌* are referred  to as *congruent*, with *ξ* = *V ![image](images/xicaron.jpg)* being the corresponding *congruence transformation*. One has *ξ*^⊤*Qξ* = *![image](images/xicaron.jpg)*^⊤*V*^⊤*QV![image](images/xicirc.jpg)* = *![image](images/xicaron.jpg)*^⊤*Q̌![image](images/xicirc.jpg)*, from which *q̌*(*![image](images/xicaron.jpg)*) = *![image](images/xicaron.jpg)*^⊤*Q̌![image](images/xicaron.jpg)* is the quadratic form associated with *Q̌*.

**Lemma 1.7.1.** *For any Q* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*), *there is V* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*), det(*V*) ≠ 0, *such that Q̌* = *V*^⊤*QV* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*) *is diagonal, with the entries on the main diagonal in the set* {−1, 0, +1}*. **Proof.** Any symmetric *Q* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*) has real eigenvalues and can be diagonalized by a linear transformation, i.e., it admits a decomposition of the form *Q* = *W* Λ*W* ^(−1), where the columns of *W* are eigenvectors of *Q* and Λ is diagonal, with the eigenvalues of *Q* on the main diagonal, Λ = diag(*λ*[1], . . . , *λ[m]*). An infinite-dimensional matrix (such as *H[σ]*) is said to have finite rank *r* if all the determinants of its minors of dimension greater than *r* are zero but there is at least one non-zero determinant of a minor of dimension *r*. Kronecker has proved that the infinite matrix *H[σ]* has finite rank if and only if and only if the formal series ![image](images/i0088-01.jpg)is convergent for all *ẑ* in a neighborhood ![image](images/capn.jpg)of *z* = 0, and its sum *σ*(*ẑ*), for *ẑ* ∈ ![image](images/capn.jpg), is a rational function of *ẑ*; in this case, the number of poles of the rational function *σ*(*z*) is *r* − 1, where *r* is the rank of matrix *H[σ]*; in particular, the leading principal minor of *H[σ]* of dimension *r* has determinant different from zero.

The *m*th *leading principal minor* of a square matrix *M* is the matrix obtained by deleting all but the first *m* rows and columns of *M*.

**Proof.** Let *q*[〈*p*〉,*h*](*ξ*) be the quadratic form associated with *T*[〈*p*〉,*h*],

![image](images/f0094-01.jpg)

Since *p* is square free, the roots *ẑ*[1], . . . , *ẑ[m]* are distinct, from which the associated Vandermonde matrix *V* (*ẑ*[1], . . . , *ẑ[m]*) is invertible, and, therefore, the *m* linear forms *ξ*[1] + *ẑ[i]ξ*[2] + · · · + ![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]* are linearly independent. One has the following cases:

(i) If *h*(*ẑ[i]*) = 0, then *h*(*ẑ[i]*)·(*ξ*[1]+*ẑ[i]ξ*[2]+· · ·+![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]*)² = 0, regardless of whether *ẑ[i]* is real or non-real.

(ii) If *ẑ[i]* is real and *h*(*ẑ[i]*) > 0, then *h*(*ẑ[i]*)·(*ξ*[1]+*ẑ[i]ξ*[2]+· · ·+![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]*)² = ![image](images/i0094-01.jpg)· (*ξ*[1] + *ẑ[i]ξ*[2] + · · · + ![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]*))² is a square of a real linear form, with coefficient +1.

(iii) If *ẑ[i]* is real and *h*(*ẑ[i]*) < 0, then *h*(*ẑ[i]*)·(*ξ*[1]+*ẑ[i]ξ*[2]+· · ·+![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]*)² = −(![image](images/i0094-02.jpg)(*ξ*[1]+*ẑ[i]ξ*[2]+· · ·+![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]*))² is a square of a real linear form, with coefficient −1.

(iv) If *ẑ[i]* is non-real and *h*(*ẑ[i]*) ≠ 0, then the sum of *h*(*ẑ[i]*)·(*ξ*[1] +*ẑ[i]ξ*[2] + · · · + ![image](images/i0089-01.jpg)*ξ[m]*)² and of its complex conjugate yields two squares of real linear forms, one with coefficient +1 and the other one with coefficient −1.

Then, (1.7.5.2) follows from (i), (1.7.5.1) follows from (iii) and (iv), and (1.7.5.3) follows from (ii) and (iv). Finally, (1.7.5.4) follows from (1.7.5.1) and (1.7.5.3).

### **1.10 Modules and syzygies**

If ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\] is the ring of the polynomials in *x*, with coefficients in the field ![image](images/kopf.jpg), then the set ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\], *m* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)1], of the vectors, whose *m* entries are polynomials in the ring ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], . . . , *x[n]*\], is a *module over the ring* ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]; in the following, the elements of the *ambient module* ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] are referred to as *polynomial vectors*. A module over a ring is a generalization of the notion of vector space over a field, where the scalars are the elements of the ring, the addition is defined between elements of the module, and the multiplication is defined between elements of the ring and elements of the module: given two polynomial vectors *p, q* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\], with entries *p[i], q[i]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], and one polynomial scalar *c* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], one has *p* + *q* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] and *cp* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\], with \[*p*+*q*\]*[i]* = *p[i]* +*q[i]*, and \[*cp*\]*[i]* = *cp[i]*, *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, where \[·\]*[i]* denotes the *i*th entry of the vector at argument.

**Definition 1.10.1.** A subset ![image](images/capm.jpg)of ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] is a *sub-module* in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] if it satisfies:

(1.10.1.1) 0 ∈ ![image](images/capm.jpg)(the zero polynomial vector belongs to ![image](images/capm.jpg)).

The polynomial vectors *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] are *generators* of the sub-module 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉. As for ideals in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], any sub-module ![image](images/capm.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] has a finite set of generators.

If *p*[1], . . . , *p[s]* are generators of some sub-module ![image](images/capm.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\], ![image](images/capm.jpg)\= 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉, then {*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*} is said to be a *basis* of ![image](images/capm.jpg), and *P* = \[*p*[1] . . . *p[s]*\] ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*s*)\[*x*\] is referred to as a *presentation matrix* of ![image](images/capm.jpg). For *P* = \[*p*[1] . . . *p[s]*\] ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*s*)\[*x*\], 〈*P*〉 is used to denote the sub-module generated by the columns of *P* (i.e., 〈*P*〉 = 〈*p*[1], . . . , *p[s]*〉).

Sub-modules of ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] can exhibit behaviors very different from vector spaces. For instance, it is well known from linear algebra that a basis of a vector space is constituted by vectors that are linearly independent and any vector in the vector space is a ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\-linear combination of these vectors. This need not be true for sub-modules of ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\], since the scalars are taken in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]. Consider, for instance, the polynomial vectors *p*[1], *p*[2], *p*[3] of [Example 1.10.1](#chapter1.xhtml#exa1-10-1). It can easily be checked that {*p*[1], *p*[2], *p*[3]} is a reduced Gröbner basis for ![image](images/capm.jpg)\= 〈*p*[1], *p*[2], *p*[3]〉 and that *c*[1](*x*) = −*x*[3], *c*[2](*x*) = *x*[2], *c*[3](*x*) = *x*[1] are such that *c*[1]*p*[1] + *c*[2]*p*[2] + *c*[3]*p*[3] is the zero polynomial vector. This example shows that, unlike vector spaces, sub-modules need not have bases that are ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]-linearly independent. More generally, no sub-module ![image](images/capm.jpg)in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)¹\[*x*\], which is not principal and non-zero, can be generated by a ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]-linearly independent set. In fact, any pair of polynomials *p*[1], *p*[2] ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\] satisfy a non-trivial ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]-linear dependence, because *p*[2]*p*[1] − *p*[1]*p*[2] = 0.

For the applications considered in this book, the following definition is needed: if ![image](images/capm.jpg)is a sub-module in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m* \[*x*\] and ![image](images/capj.jpg)is an ideal in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\], then the *quotient* of ![image](images/capm.jpg)by ![image](images/capj.jpg)is the set

![image](images/f0127-07.jpg)

which is a sub-module of ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\].

## **Chapter 2**

## **Implementations in Macaulay2**

### **2.1 The Macaulay2 language**

Most of the computations reported in this book have been carried out using `Macaulay2` (Grayson and Stillman, 2020), a free, open-source computer algebra system for computations in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. The objective of this chapter is to provide some snippets of code, to introduce the reader to the use of `Macaulay2`. This is far from being a complete and general introduction to this system, but it is rather an applicative commentary to the theory resumed in [Chapter 1](#chapter1.xhtml).

To do polynomial computations with `Macaulay2`, one must fix the ambient ring to which the polynomials belong and fix a monomial order on it. For instance, to fix the ambient ring ![image](images/qopf.jpg)\[*x*[1], . . . , *x*[4]\] and the Lex monomial order, with *x*[1] ≻[Lex] . . . ≻[Lex] *x*[4], one can use the following input instruction:

`i1 : R = QQ[x_1..x_4, MonomialOrder => Lex]`

where `i1` represents the input prompt; executing this instruction generates two lines of output labeled `o1` showing the name of the output

`o1 = R`

and the type of the output:

`o1 : PolynomialRing`

The `QQ` is the `Macaulay2` instruction for the field ![image](images/qopf.jpg)(the fields ![image](images/ropf.jpg)and ![image](images/copf.jpg)of the real and complex numbers, respectively, are represented by `RR` and `CC`), whereas `Lex` stands for the Lex monomial order (the GRL monomial order is fixed by `GRevLex`, whereas the elimination order that eliminates the first `i` variables from the start of the list is fixed by `MonomialOrder => Elimination i`). The order on the ring variables is specified by the list in the square brackets.

Once any monomial order on the ambient ring has been chosen, the polynomials *p*[1](*x*) = *x*[1] − ![image](images/x22.jpg)\+ *x*[3] and *p*[2](*x*) = ![image](images/x41.jpg)\+ *x*[2]![image](images/x23.jpg)\+ *x*[4] are assigned to `p1` and `p2`, respectively, with the instructions:

`p1 = x_1-x_2^2+x_3`

`p2 = x_1^4+x_2*x_3^2+x_4`

Then, the ideal 〈*p*[1], *p*[2]〉 is assigned to `I` with the instruction:

`I = ideal(p1,p2)`

whereas

`G = gens gb I`

computes the reduced Gröbner basis of `I` and assign to `G` the result as a one-row matrix of polynomials.

The remainder of the division of the polynomial ![image](images/x21.jpg)+![image](images/x22.jpg)+![image](images/x23.jpg)+![image](images/x24.jpg)−1 by ![image](images/capi.jpg)is computed by

`(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2-1) % I`

`Macaulay2` allows very general coefficient fields in polynomial rings. For instance, to fix the polynomial ring ![image](images/qopf.jpg)(*u*[1], *u*[2])\[*x*[1], *x*[2]\] (i.e., the ring of polynomials in *x*[1], *x*[2], with coefficients in the field of the rational functions ![image](images/qopf.jpg)(*u*[1], *u*[2])) and the GRL monomial order, with *x*[2] ≻[GRL] *x*[1], the following instruction can be used:

`R = frac(QQ[u_1,u_2])[x_2,x_1, MonomialOrder => GRevLex]`

Quotient rings can be fixed in `Macaulay2` as well. For instance, the ring ![image](images/qopf.jpg)\[*x*[1]\]/〈![image](images/x21.jpg)\+ 1〉 is fixed as

`QR = QQ[x_1]/ideal(x_1^2+1)`

The leading term, leading monomial, and leading coefficient of a polynomial (with respect to the chosen monomial order) are computed by `leadTerm`, `leadMonomial`, and `leadCoefficient`, respectively. The `leadTerm` instruction can also be applied to an ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)and the output is a set of generators for 〈LT(![image](images/capi.jpg))〉.

`Macaulay2` can carry out also operations on ideals. Hence, if the ideals ![image](images/capi.jpg)and ![image](images/capj.jpg)are represented by `I` and `J`, one can compute

• the sum of ![image](images/capi.jpg)and ![image](images/capj.jpg)as `I+J`,

• the product of ![image](images/capi.jpg)and ![image](images/capj.jpg)as `I*J`,

• the intersection of ![image](images/capi.jpg)and ![image](images/capj.jpg)as `intersect(I,J)`,

• the quotient of ![image](images/capi.jpg)by ![image](images/capj.jpg)as `I:J`,

• the saturation of ![image](images/capi.jpg)by ![image](images/capj.jpg)as `saturate(I,J)`.

The radical of the ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)represented by `I` is computed and its generators are presented by

`gens radical(I)`

The above instruction returns a set of generators of the radical of the ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)represented by `I` as a row vector.

`Macaulay2` is also able to carry out operations on modules and sub-modules. Before working with a sub-module in ![image](images/kopf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\], the base ring has to be fixed as in the case of polynomial ideals. To fix the Lex monomial order, with the TOP[⇓] extension, as it has been introduced in [Section 1.10](#chapter1.xhtml#sec1-10), one can use the instruction `MonomialOrder =>` {`Lex, Position => Down`}, whereas the POT[⇓] extension of the GRL monomial order can be fixed with the instruction `MonomialOrder =>` {`Position => Down, GRevLex`}. As for polynomial ideals, the order on the ring variables is specified by the list in the square brackets.

The presentation matrix of a sub-module can be obtained through the instruction `matrix`. For instance, the matrix

![image](images/f0131-01.jpg)

can be set through the instruction

`P = matrix{{x_1^2+x_2,x_1-x_3,x_4},{x_2^2+x_1, 0,-x_3}}`

Then, the sub-module whose presentation matrix is *P* can be generated as

`M = image P`

The reduced Gröbner basis of the module `M` with respect to the chosen monomial order can be computed using the instruction

`gens gb M`

which returns the reduced Gröbner basis of `M` through the corresponding presentation matrix. Finally, a syzygy matrix of `P` can be computed as

`syz P`

## **Chapter 3**

## **The Inverse Kinematics of Robot Arms**

### **3.1 The direct kinematics**

A robot arm can be represented by a set of *n*+1 rigid links connected by *n* joints (either of rotational or linear type, with one degree of freedom). The links are the rigid members connecting the joints, and the joints are the movable parts of the robot that cause relative motion between adjacent links. If the joints are of linear type, then the relative motion between adjacent links is a translation, whereas, if the joints are of rotational type, then the relative motion is a rotation. Let the links of the robot be numbered from 0 to *n* (the 0th link is the base of the robot, whereas the *n*th link corresponds to the endeffector). The joints are numbered from 1 to *n*: the *i*th joint connects the (*i* − 1)th link with the *i*th one, *i* = 1, 2, . . . , *n*. The generalized coordinate representing the displacement of the *i*th joint is *q[i]*: *q[i]* is a distance if the *i*th joint is of linear type, whereas *q[i]* is an angle if the *i*th joint is of rotational type. Define *n*+1 reference frames, each one attached to one link: the reference frame ![image](images/capr.jpg)*[i]* is attached to the *i*th link, *i* = 0, 1, . . . , *n*, so that ![image](images/capr.jpg)[0] is an inertial frame, and the origin of ![image](images/capr.jpg)*[n]* is located on the end-effector.

**Example 3.1.1.** Consider the robot arm depicted in [Figure 3.1](#chapter3.xhtml#fig3-1) with three rotational links. In such a figure, the symbol ◦ (respectively, ×) denotes a vector orthogonal to the plane of representation that exits from (respectively, enters in) such a plane. This notation is  used for all robotic structures reported hereafter. Note that the links are numbered from 0 (base of the robot) to 3 (end-effector) and that the joints are numbered from 1 to 3. Namely, the joint whose generalized coordinate is *q*[1] (respectively, *q*[2], *q*[3]) connects the 0th and 1st (respectively, the 1st and the 2nd, the 2nd and the 3rd) links. The reference frame ![image](images/capr.jpg)[0](*x*[0], *y*[0], *z*[0]) is attached to the 0th link and, hence, it is an inertial frame. On the other hand, the reference frame ![image](images/capr.jpg)[3](*x*[3], *y*[3], *z*[3]) is attached to the end-effector.

![image](images/fig3-1.jpg)

Fig. 3.1: A robot with an *anthropomorphic* arm-and-body section.

**Example 3.1.2.** Consider the robot arm of [Example 3.1.1](#chapter3.xhtml#exa3-1-1). The transformation matrices among the reference frames ![image](images/capr.jpg)[0], . . . , ![image](images/capr.jpg)[3] are

which are such that *Q*[0,2] = *Q*[0,1]*Q*[1,2], and *Q*[0,3] = *Q*[0,2]*Q*[2,3]. In particular, note that the vector

![image](images/f0146-01.jpg)

is the position of the end-effector with respect to the reference frame ![image](images/capr.jpg)[0].

One of the most commonly used methods to place the reference frames ![image](images/capr.jpg)[0], . . . , ![image](images/capr.jpg)*[n]* is the *Denavit–Hartenberg procedure*, which is summarized in [Algorithm 3.1.1](#chapter3.xhtml#alg3-1-1).

Algorithm 3.1.1: Denavit–Hartenberg procedure.

![image](images/alg3-1-1.jpg)

If the Denavit–Hartenberg procedure outlined in [Algorithm 3.1.1](#chapter3.xhtml#alg3-1-1) is used in the collocation of the reference frames, each transformation matrix *Q*[*i*−1*,i*] is the product of *four elementary transformation matrices*, depending on four parameters (*θ[i], d[i], α[i], a[i]*):

![image](images/eq3-1.jpg)

this corresponds to a rotation about the *z*\-axis of an angle *θ[i]*, followed by a translation along the *z*\-axis of a displacement *d[i]*, followed by a rotation about the *x*\-axis of an angle *α[i]*, followed by a translation along the *x*\-axis of a displacement *a*. This means that the relative motion of two adjacent links is described by the following parameters:

(i) *θ[i]* is the *joint angle*,

(ii) *d[i]* is the *link offset*,

(iii) *α[i]* is the *link twist*,

(iv) *a[i]* is the *link length*.

When dealing with robot arms, these parameters can be summarized in a table, referred to as the *Denavit–Hartenberg table*, that summarizes the sequence of elementary operations (i.e., rotations and translations) required to move the reference frame ![image](images/capr.jpg)[0] into the reference frame ![image](images/capr.jpg)*[n]*.

Most robot arms can be divided into two parts: the first part is the arm-and-body section, with three degrees of freedom; the second part is usually a spherical wrist, with three degrees of freedom. The aim of the arm-and-body section is to locate the end-effector of the robot at some point of the workspace, whereas the aim of the spherical wrist is to give the orientation to the robot end-effector. In fact, when dealing with most robot arms, the position and orientation direct kinematics can be decoupled through the following steps:

(1) given the desired position and orientation of the end effector, determine the target position of the arm-and-body section;

(2) solve the position inverse kinematics problem for the arm-andbody section;

(3) considering the orientation resulting from the solution to the position inverse kinematics and the target orientation, solve the orientation inverse kinematics problem for the spherical wrist.

Therefore, in most cases, the position and orientation direct kinematics can be considered disjointedly, as in this chapter.

In [Section 3.2](#chapter3.xhtml#sec3-2), only the arm-and-body section is considered, and the corresponding direct kinematics is constituted by the following three equations:

![image](images/f0148-01.jpg)

where *ξ* is a vector having the coordinates (*x, y, z*) as entries.

The problem of determining the inverse orientation is instead considered in [Section 3.4](#chapter3.xhtml#sec3-4).

### **3.2 The inverse kinematics**

Solving the inverse kinematics problem consists in finding the solutions in closed-form of the following system of equations:

![image](images/eq3-2.jpg)

possibly containing some trigonometric terms, where *β* is the vector representing the physical parameters of the robot, *q* is the vector of  the joint generalized coordinates, and *ξ* = \[*x y z*\] is the vector of the end-effector coordinates. The function *h* can directly be determined by inspecting the matrix *Q*[0,3] (in particular, the entries corresponding to *d*[0,3], considered as functions of the physical parameters *β* of the robot arm and of the joint generalized coordinates *q*). Solving the inverse kinematics means finding all joints generalized coordinates *q* such that the end-effector is in the desired location in the workspace, where the workspace is the set of all positions that can be reached.

The techniques outlined in [Chapter 1](#chapter1.xhtml) can directly be used to perform such a task. In fact, assume, without loss of generality, that the joint generalized coordinates are ordered so that *q*[1], . . . , *q*[*n*] correspond to rotational joints and *q*[*n*+1], . . . , *q[n]* correspond to linear joints, *n̄* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0], 0 ![image](images/le.jpg)*n̄* ![image](images/le.jpg)*n*. In view of (3.1), if the convention of Denavit–Hartenberg is used in the collocation of the reference frames, one has that *h* is a three-dimensional vector function whose entries are polynomial functions in the variables *q*[*n̄*+1], . . . , *q[n]* and trigonometric functions in the variables *q*[1], . . . , *q*[*n̄*].

Although the functions cos(·) and sin(·) are not polynomials, the map

![image](images/f0149-01.jpg)

constitute a parameterization of the variety **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*c*² + *s*² − 1) in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)². Therefore, by repeated applications of the formulas

![image](images/f0149-02.jpg)

and applying, for *i* = 1, . . . , *n̄*, the substitutions

![image](images/f0149-03.jpg)

the forward kinematics (3.2) can equivalently be rewritten as

![image](images/eq3-3a.jpg)

with *p*[1], *p*[2], *p*[3] ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)(*β, x, y, z*)\[*c*[1], *s*[1], . . . , *c*[*n̄*], *s*[*n̄*], *q*[*n̄*+1], . . . , *q[n]*\]. Thus, considering the following ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)(*β, x, y, z*)\[*c*[1], *s*[1], . . . , *c*[*n̄*], *s*[*n̄*], *q*[*n̄*+1], . . . , *q[n]*\]:

![image](images/eq3-4.jpg)

the methods outlined in [Chapter 1](#chapter1.xhtml) can be used to determine the set of all joints configurations *q* such that the end-effector is in the desired location *ξ* = \[*x y z*\]^⊤, for “almost all” *ξ* in the workspace and “almost all” physical parameters *β* of the robot arm. In fact, using the procedures outlined in [Chapter 1](#chapter1.xhtml), one can determine a reduced Gröbner basis of the ideal ![image](images/capi.jpg)that can be used to find closedform algebraic inverses of the direct kinematics (3.2). In particular, these expressions can be used at all the points within the workspace wherein the denominator of the rational expressions do not vanish and the arguments of the square roots are positive. Since the algebraic set satisfying these properties is open, these inverses can be used for almost all *ξ* in the workspace and “almost all” physical parameters *β* of the robot arm, according to [Definition 1.1.2](#chapter1.xhtml#def1-1-2).

The following section shows how this technique can be used to determine the inverse kinematics of some well-known arm-and-body structures.

### **4.8 Fault detection and isolation for a DC motor**

The problem of fault detection and isolation for a permanent-magnet direct current (DC) motor is considered in this section. The fault detection and isolation method considered in this section is *model-based*; in particular, it is assumed that:

(i) The dynamic behavior of a DC motor is described, both if the motor is in a *nominal condition* (i.e., no fault has occurred) and if the motor is in a *faulty condition* (i.e., a fault has occurred), by the same nonlinear dynamic system, but characterized by different parameters.

(ii) The nonlinear dynamic system depends on a vector *β* of some parameters. There are a finite number of nominal and faulty conditions, each one identified by a different vector *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*; if *β* = *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦ (*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦ is the vector of the *nominal parameters*), the DC motor is in the nominal condition, whereas if *β* = *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i*, *i* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)1] (*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i* is the vector of the *faulty parameters* in the *i*th faulty condition), the DC motor is in the *i*th faulty condition.

(iii) For each *i* ≠ *j*, one has *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i* ≠ *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^j*; in addition, for each fault *i*, one and only one entry of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i* differs from the corresponding entry of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, from which the maximum number of possible faults is equal to the number of parameters. The values of the entries of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^◦* are known, whereas the value of the entry of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i* being different from the corresponding entry of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦ is unknown, taking a faulty value.

Similarly, if the fault corresponding too *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i* has occurred, one has that |*g*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i,* ![image](images/i0219-01.jpg)(*t*))| ![image](images/le.jpg)*ϵ*.  Unfortunately, since the value of *![image](images/betacirc.jpg)^i* is not known, the use of the polynomial *g* does not allow one to detect which failure has occurred, but only that one of the faults has occurred.

Therefore, a “Fault Detector” can be obtained through the following reasoning.

Let *ϵ* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg), *ϵ* > 0, be a threshold value. If |*g*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| ![image](images/le.jpg)*ϵ*, one concludes that the DC motor is in the nominal condition, whereas if |*g*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| > *ϵ*, one concludes that the DC motor is in a faulty condition. In particular, when |*g*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| > *ϵ*, which failure has occurred can be deduced by determining which, among the functions |*g[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg))|, *i* ∈ {1, . . . , 7}, assumes the smaller value. As a matter of fact, by construction, if the fault corresponding to the perturbation of the parameter *β[i]*, *i* ∈ {1, . . . , 7}, has occurred, the corresponding output embedding *g[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg)) is identically zero, whereas all others output embeddings *g[j]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg)), *j* ≠ *i*, are different from zero. Therefore, which failure has occurred can be determined by finding out which output embedding assumes the smallest absolute value when evaluated on ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg). Once one has determined which fault has occurred, say the *i*th one, an estimate *x̌*[2](*t*) of the state variable *x*[2](*t*) can be determined through the formula *x̌*[2](*t*) = *w[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg)).

Hence, a vector *ϕ*(*t*) ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)² can be defined as follows:

1. The entry *ϕ*[1](*t*) is 

(a) equal to 0, if |*g*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| ![image](images/le.jpg)*ϵ*, from which one concludes that the motor is in the nominal condition;

(b) equal to *i*, if |*g*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| > *ϵ*, |*g[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| ![image](images/le.jpg)*ϵ* and |*g[j]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-04.jpg))| > *ϵ*, for all *j* ≠ *i*, from which one concludes that the motor is in the faulty condition corresponding to a sufficiently high perturbation of the parameter *β[i]*;

(c) equal to −1, in all the other cases, from which one concludes that the faulty condition has not been identified.

2. The entry *ϕ*[2](*t*) is 

(a) equal to 0, if either *ϕ*[1](*t*) = −1 or *ϕ*[1](*t*) = *i* but the formula *x̌*[2](*t*) = *w[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg)) cannot be applied, for instance when the denominator of *w[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg)) is too close to zero;

(b) equal to the estimate *x̌*[2](*t*) = *w[i]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, ![image](images/i0221-05.jpg)) of the state variable *x*[2](*t*), otherwise.

### **5.3 Immersion into LIS form up to a finite order**

By [Remark 5.2.1](#chapter5.xhtml#rem5-2-1), the coefficients of the expressions given in [Tables 5.1](#chapter5.xhtml#tab5-1) and [5.2](#chapter5.xhtml#tab5-2) provide necessary and sufficient conditions for solvability of [Problem 5.1.1](#chapter5.xhtml#pro5-1-1) through [Algorithm 5.2.2](#chapter5.xhtml#alg5-2-2). However, if  such conditions do not hold, it may still be possible to compute an immersion that recasts the polynomial system (5.1) into the LIS form (5.2), apart from higher-order terms. Namely, system (5.1) is *LIS up to order d* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0], if it can be recast into a system of the form *ż*(*t*) = *f̃*(*z*)(*t*), where *f̃* : ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^ν* → ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^ν* is such that its Taylor expansion up to order *d*, denoted *f̃[d]*, is

![image](images/eq5-8.jpg)

for some mapping *ψ[i]* : ![image](images/ropf.jpg)→ ![image](images/ropf.jpg), *i* = 1, . . . , *ν*. Clearly, if system (5.1) is LIS, then it is LIS up to order *d*, for any *d* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0], whereas the converse need not hold (see, e.g., [Example 5.3.1](#chapter5.xhtml#exa5-3-1), where a system that is not LIS, but is LIS up to order 3, is given).

Hence, consider the following problem.

**Problem 5.3.1.** *Let system* (5.1) *and d* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0], *be given. Find, if any, an immersion* (*τ, θ*) *that recasts system* (5.1) *in LIS form up to order d.*

The following assumption is made to solve [Problem 5.3.1](#chapter5.xhtml#pro5-3-1).

**Assumption 5.3.1.** Let *f*(0) = 0 and *h*(0) = 0.

Under such an assumption, one has that, by the continuity of the observability map *O[N]* , for any *δ* > 0 there is a neighborhood ![image](images/capu.jpg)of the origin such that ||*O[N]* (*x̂*)|| < *δ* for all *x̂* ∈ ![image](images/capu.jpg). Hence, let *p* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*y[e,N]*\] be an output embedding of system (5.1) and consider *p*(*εy[e,N]*) ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*y[e,N] , ε*\], where *ε* is an auxiliary single variable. The Taylor series of *p*(*εy[e,N]*) about *ε* = 0, truncated at order *d*, is the sum

where *p[i]* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*y[e,N]*\] is homogeneous of total degree *i*, *i* = 1, . . . , *d*. ### **6.2 The method of the Lagrange multipliers**

The method of the Lagrange multipliers for the computation of the extremum points of a function subject to some equality constraints can be introduced as follows.

Suppose that *f*(*x*) and *g*(*x*) are differentiable single functions on the whole ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n*, with continuous partial derivatives, let *J[f]* = ![image](images/i0248-01.jpg)and *J[g]* = ![image](images/i0248-02.jpg), and denote *J[f,i]* and *J[g,i]* their entries, respectively. Assume that the problem is to find a local maximum *f*^⋆ of *f* (finding a local minimum of *f* is equivalent to find a local maximum of −*f*) subject to the constraint *g* = 0,

![image](images/eq6-2.jpg)

Let *x̂*^⋆ ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n* be such that *f*(*x̂*^⋆) = *f*^⋆.

Under the assumption that *J[g]*(*x̂*^⋆) ≠ 0, the method of the Lagrange multipliers consists in introducing a new function (called the *Lagrange function* and considered as a function of (*x, λ*)),

![image](images/f0248-02.jpg)

which incorporates both the function to be maximized and the constraint, where *λ* is an additional single variable, called a *Lagrange multiplier*. Under some conditions, *x̂*^⋆ is a solution to problem (6.2) only if it is an unconstrained critical point of *f[e]* (it is noted that *f[e]* need not have an unconstrained local maximum, although one is assuming that *f* subject to the constraint *g* = 0 has a local maximum).

The reasoning given in the previous page can be justified as follows. Suppose that *x* = *X*(*ℓ*), where *ℓ* is a single variable, is a parameterization of the constraint around the constrained local maximum, i.e., *g*(*X*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*)) = 0, for all *![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)* ∈ ![image](images/capl.jpg), where ![image](images/capl.jpg)is an open interval in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)having *![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆ as an interior point, and *X*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆) = *x̂*^⋆. Let *F*(*ℓ*) = *f*(*X*(*ℓ*)) and *G*(*ℓ*) = *g*(*X*(*ℓ*)). Since *G*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*) = 0, for all *![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)* ∈ ![image](images/capl.jpg), one has *J[g]*(*X*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*)) *· X′*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*) = 0, for all *![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*∈ ![image](images/capl.jpg), where *X′* = ![image](images/i0249-01.jpg). Since, by construction, *f*^⋆ is the unconstrained local maximum of *F*(*ℓ*), one has ![image](images/i0249-02.jpg)\= 0, from which *J[f]*(*X*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆)) *· X′*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆) = 0. Roughly speaking, under the assumption that *X′*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆) ≠ 0, from the above reasoning, one has that the vectors ![image](images/i0249-03.jpg)(*X*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆)) and ![image](images/i0249-04.jpg)(*X*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆)) are both perpendicular to *X′*(*![image](images/lscrcirc.jpg)*^⋆), and, therefore, are parallel; hence, there exist ![image](images/i0249-05.jpg)∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg), with (![image](images/i0249-05.jpg)) ≠ (0, 0), such that

![image](images/eq6-3.jpg)

Since *J[f]* points to the direction of steepest increase of *f*, *J[f]* can be thought of as the “good direction”, whereas *J[g]* can be thought of as the “bad direction”, because following the direction *J[g]* the constraint is violated. **Definition 6.3.1.** The following set is referred to as a *semi-algebraic set*:

![image](images/f0266-01.jpg)

Finite unions and intersections of semi-algebraic sets are semi-algebraic. In addition, unlike affine varieties, the complement of a semi-algebraic set is semi-algebraic. Finally, the projection of a semi-algebraic set onto a linear space is semi-algebraic; in particular, also the projection of an affine variety (which is also a semi-algebraic set) onto a linear space is semi-algebraic. Actually, in the following, it is shown that any semi-algebraic set can be thought of as the projection of some affine variety.

Letting *ℓ* be a dummy single-variable and *π[x]* be the projection map which sends (*ℓ, x*) to *x*, one has

(1) **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p*(*x*) ≠ 0) = *π[x]*(**V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*ℓ · p* − 1));

 (2) **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p*(*x*) > 0) = *π[x]*(**V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*ℓ*² *· p* − 1));

(3) **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p*(*x*) < 0) = *π[x]*(**V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*ℓ*² *· p* + 1));

(4) **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p*(*x*) ![image](images/ge.jpg)0) = *π[x]*(**V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p* − *ℓ*²));

(5) **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p*(*x*) ![image](images/le.jpg)0) = *π[x]*(**V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p* + *ℓ*²)).

Hence, given the set of relations {*p*[1] ♯ 0, . . . , *p[s] ♯* 0}, there exist polynomials *q*[1], . . . , *q[r]* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*ℓ, x*\], where *ℓ* is a dummy multiple–variable, such that the semi-algebraic set **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*p*[1] ♯ 0, . . . , *p[s] ♯* 0) can be expressed as the projection *π[x]*(**V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*q*[1], . . . , *q[r]*)) of an affine variety **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*q*[1], . . . , *q[r]*),

**Example 6.6.6.** Consider the same juggler of [Example 6.6.1](#chapter6.xhtml#exa6-6-1). In the following computations, the values *m*[1] = 1 kg, *m*[2] = 20 kg, *m*[3] = 2 kg, *m*[4] = 1 kg, *k*[1] = 10 N/m, *k*[2] = 5 N/m, ![image](images/qdot.jpg)(0) = \[0.1 0.3\]^⊤m, ![image](images/qdot.jpg)*[C]*(0) = \[0.2 0.4\]^⊤m/s, *q[N]* (0) = −![image](images/qdot.jpg)(0) and ![image](images/qdot.jpg)*[N]* (0) = −*q[N]* (0) have been assumed.

[Algorithms 6.6.1](#chapter6.xhtml#alg6-6-1) and the technique outlined in [Theorem 6.6.1](#chapter6.xhtml#the6-6-1) have been used to compute a feedback control law which solves the dead-beat regulation problem, for two different values of the parameter *L*.

Namely, such techniques have been used to solve the dead-beat regulation problem for *L* = 1m, *H* = 4*n[N]* − 1 = 7, and a simulation has been carried out to test the proposed feedback control law. [Figures 6.7(a)](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-7) and [6.7(b)](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-7) show the signal *y*(*t*) = ![image](images/jcaron.jpg)*[q]*(*t*) and the states ![image](images/qdot.jpg)(*t*) and *q[N]* (*t*) of the closed-loop system, respectively.

![image](images/fig6-7.jpg)

Fig. 6.7: Simulation of the solution to the dead-beat regulation problem, with respect to the juggler in [Figure 6.6](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-6), for *L* = 1m.

![image](images/fig6-8.jpg)

Fig. 6.8: Simulation of the solution to the dead-beat regulation problem, with respect to the juggler in [Figure 6.6](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-6), for *L* = 0.08m.

A solution to the dead-beat regulation problem has been computed also for *L* = 0.08 m. In such a case, the technique outlined in [Theorem 6.6.1](#chapter6.xhtml#the6-6-1) is not able to find a polynomial *y[d]* which satisfies (6.16)–(6.18) for *H* = 7. However, for *H* = 8, a solution to the deadbeat regulation problem can be computed. A simulation has been carried out to test the proposed feedback control law. [Figures 6.8(a)](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-8) and [6.8(b)](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-8) show the signal *y*(*t*) = ![image](images/jcaron.jpg)*[q]*(*t*) and the states ![image](images/qdot.jpg)(*t*) and *q[N]* (*t*) of system (6.10), respectively. As [Figues 6.7](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-7) and [6.8](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6-8) show, after *T[f]* = 4s, one has that *q[N]* (*t*) = 0, and ![image](images/qdot.jpg)*[N]* (*t*) = 0, for all times *t* > *T[f]* .

Since *f* does not depend on time *t*, without loss of generality, by a shift of the time axis, the initial time *t^◦* is always taken equal to 0 in the following. The *solution x*(*t*) of the DT-system (8.9) from the initial state *x*(0) = *x^◦* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n* is *x*(*t*) = *ψ[f]* (*t, x^◦*), where *ψ[f]* (*t, x*) is the *t*th iteration of *f*(*x*) (i.e., *ψ[f]* (0, *x*) = *x*, *ψ[f]* (1, *x*) = *f*(*x*), *ψ[f]* (2, *x*) = *f ◦ f*(*x*), and so on), with *t* ∈ ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0]. The are no questions about the existence and uniqueness of solution for real analytic DT-systems, in the sense that the solution *x*(*t*) is defined on the whole ![image](images/zopf.jpg)[![image](images/subge.jpg)0] and is uniquely determined by the initial state *x^◦* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n*. The function *ψ[f]* : ![image](images/zopf.jpg)〈 ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n* → ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n* is the *DT-flow* associated with *f* and satisfies (Menini and Tornambe, 2011)

Unlike CT-systems (i.e., systems represented by differential equations), existence and uniqueness of the solution is only ensured for the forward direction of time, since *f* need not be injective.

## **Chapter 9**

## **Boolean Networks**

### **9.1 The Galois field** ![image](images/fopf.jpg)**[2]**

Let *a* and *b* be arbitrary integers; *a* is congruent to *b* modulo 2 (denoted *a* = *b* mod 2) if the difference *a*−*b* is a multiple of 2. Hence, ![image](images/zopf.jpg)can be partitioned into two congruence classes, ![image](images/odbra.jpg)0![image](images/cdbra.jpg)and ![image](images/odbra.jpg)1![image](images/cdbra.jpg), of all integers congruent to 0 and to 1 modulo 2, respectively. It is possible to define the sum and the product of two congruence classes as ![image](images/odbra.jpg)*a*![image](images/cdbra.jpg)\+ ![image](images/odbra.jpg)*b*![image](images/cdbra.jpg)\= ![image](images/odbra.jpg)*a* + *b*![image](images/cdbra.jpg)and ![image](images/odbra.jpg)*ab*![image](images/cdbra.jpg)\= ![image](images/odbra.jpg)*a*![image](images/cdbra.jpg)![image](images/odbra.jpg)*b*![image](images/cdbra.jpg), respectively. Hence, the set {![image](images/odbra.jpg)0![image](images/cdbra.jpg), ![image](images/odbra.jpg)1![image](images/cdbra.jpg)}, with the sum and the product defined above, is a finite field and is denoted ![image](images/zopf.jpg)/2.

Let ![image](images/fopf.jpg)[2] := {0, 1} and let *φ* : ![image](images/zopf.jpg)/2 → ![image](images/fopf.jpg)[2] be the mapping defined by *φ*(![image](images/odbra.jpg)*a*![image](images/cdbra.jpg)) = *a*, for *a* ∈ {0, 1}. One has that ![image](images/fopf.jpg)[2], with the field structure induced by *φ*, is a finite field, which is called the *Galois field of order 2*.

Let *x* = \[*x*[1] . . . *x[n]*\]^⊤ be a vector of single variables taking values in ![image](images/fn2.jpg), *i.e*., *x̂[i]* ∈ ![image](images/fopf.jpg)[2], *i* = 1, . . . , *n*; *x* is called a *Boolean vector*. #### **9.2.1 *Reduced linear representation of Boolean networks***

Although the representation through linear immersion of Boolean networks given in (9.5) has several advantages (as, e.g., the possibility of computing the solutions in closed form of the Boolean network and the availability of efficient tools to determine cycles), it has a major drawback: the size of the state. As a matter of fact, system (9.5) has 2*^n* states, whence the dimension of system (9.5) grows exponentially with the number of Boolean variables involved in the network. In order to overcome this issue, it is possible to use algebraic geometry to obtain a reduced linear representation of the Boolean network.

**Example 9.2.8.** Th-lymphocytes (or Th-cells) are a sub-type of white blood cells that play a crucial role in the adaptive immune system. They support the activity of other immune cells by secreting small proteins (called cytokines), which assist and regulate the active immune response. Such cells, when subject to proper stimulation, can differentiate into Th1 or Th2 cells, which enable cell mediated immunity and humoral responses, respectively, by secreting different cytokines.

The main objective of this example is to analyze the Boolean network modeling the Th-lymphocyte differentiation. Such a Boolean network involves *n* = 12 Boolean state variables which represent presence/absence of regulatory factors (T-bet, GATA-3) signaling transduction factors (STAT1, STAT4, STAT6, SOCS-1), lymphokines (IFN-*γ*, IL-4, IL-12) and receptors (IFN-*γ*R, IL-4R, IL-12R). [Figure 9.1](#chapter9.xhtml#fig9-1) depicts the wiring diagram of the Th-lymphocyte differentiation network.

### **9.3 Finite-horizon optimal control for Boolean networks**

In this section, a method to find a feedback control law that minimizes a finite-horizon cost function for a Boolean network is given exploiting the dynamic programming algorithm given in Bertsekas (1995) and adapted to Boolean networks in Menini *et al*. (2016a).

Before discussing the actual procedure to solve this class of optimal control problems, an algebraic geometry procedure to compute the solution to an integer programming problem is reviewed.

This assumption has been made for simplicity, but it can be removed through minor modifications of the subsequent [Problems 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1) and [10.1.2](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-2).

#### **10.1.1 *Pole placement with compensators having a fixed structure***

Let *W* (*s, x*) be the transfer matrix of the feedback control system obtained through the interconnection of *F*(*s*) and some controller having a fixed structure *G*(*s, x*), where *x* = \[*x*[1] . . . *x[n]*\]^⊤ ∈ Ω*[p]* is a vector of design parameters and Ω*[p]* is a semi-algebraic set. This class of closed-loop systems includes plants that are controlled through static output feedback, standard regulators, and so on. Let *d*(*s, x*) be the monic least common multiple of the denominators of the entries of *W* (*s, x*), which is a polynomial in *s* with coefficients being polynomials in *x*.

**Problem 10.1.1.** *Let* Ω*[p]* ⊆ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n be a given semi-algebraic set and let d*(*s, x*) *be a polynomial in s and x with real coefficients, of degree μ in s, d*(*s, x*) = *s^μ* + ![image](images/i0398-01.jpg)*c[i]*(*x*)*s*^(*μ*−*i*), *where the coefficients c*[1](*x*), . . . , *c[μ]*(*x*) *are polynomials in x, not necessarily monic. Let d̂*(*s*) = *s[μ]* + ![image](images/i0398-01.jpg)*ĉ[i]s*[*μ*−*i*], *ĉ*[1], . . . , *ĉμ* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg), *be a given Hurwitz monic polynomial. Let* ![image](images/picap.jpg)[1], . . . , ![image](images/picap.jpg)*[μ]* ∈ ![image](images/copf.jpg)*be the* (*possibly, repeated*) *roots of d̂*(*s*)*. Find, if any, x[◦]* ∈ Ω*p such that d*(*s, x[◦]*) *is Hurwitz and the following* (*non-equivalent*) *statements holds* (*possibly, in the Pareto sense as formalized in the subsequent* [*Definition* 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#def10-3-1)):

(10.1.1.a) *the real parts of the roots of d*(*s, x*) *attain minimum values at x* = *x^◦;*

(10.1.1.b) *the squared distances between one root of d*(*s, x*) *and* ![image](images/picap.jpg)[1], *between another root of d*(*s, x*) *and* ![image](images/picap.jpg)[2], . . . , *and between the remaining root of d*(*s, x*) *and* ![image](images/picap.jpg)*[μ] attain minimum values at x* = *x^◦;*

(10.1.1.c) *the squared distances* (*c[i]*(*x*) − *ĉ[i]*)2, *i* = 1, . . . , *μ, attain minimum values at x* = *x^◦*.

Note that no ordering on the roots of *d*(*s, x*) is assumed in Statement (10.1.1.b) of [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1).

If one is able to determine a solution to Statement (10.1.1.a) of [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1), feasible design parameters that achieve fast convergence of the system state solution to zero are obtained; if one is able to determine a solution to either Statements (10.1.1.b) or (10.1.1.c) of [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1), the poles of the closed-loop system are placed as  close as possible to some target values![image](images/picap.jpg)[1], . . . , ![image](images/picap.jpg)*[μ]*. Although similar, Statements (10.1.1.b) and (10.1.1.c) of [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1) need not have the same solutions (Menini *et al*., 2018b). If *μ* > *n*, there need not be *x^◦* ∈ Ω*[p]* that satisfies either Statements (10.1.1.a), (10.1.1.b) or (10.1.1.c) of [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1), and, hence, solutions to [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1) have to be understood in the Pareto sense, as in the subsequent [Definition 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#def10-3-1) (given in [Section 10.3](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3)).
