### **10.2 Scalar optimization via algebraic geometry techniques**

In this section, several preliminary results that are used in the subsequent [Section 10.3](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3) are given.

#### **10.2.1 *Path-connected semi-algebraic sets***

A set ![image](images/caps.jpg)⊆ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n* is *path-connected* if, for any *x̂, ŷ* ∈ ![image](images/caps.jpg), there is a continuous *f* : \[0, 1\] → ![image](images/caps.jpg)such that *f*(0) = *x̂* and *f*(1) = *ŷ*.

Consider the following two lemmas.

**Lemma 10.2.1.** *Any non-empty semi-algebraic set of* ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n can be decomposed as the union of a finite number of path-connected semi-algebraic sets of* ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n*.

**Proof.** By Bochnak *et al*. (2013, Proposition 2.4.13) a semi-algebraic set of ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n* is connected if and only if it is path-connected. The lemma follows from Bochnak *et al*. (2013, Theorem 2.4.5).

![image](images/squ.jpg)

**Lemma 10.2.2.** *Let p* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\]*. If a semi-algebraic set* Ω*[p] of* ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n is path-connected, then its image through p*(·), Ω*[v]* = *p*(Ω*[p]*) ⊆ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^m, is path-connected*.

**Proof.** Let *z[a]* and *z[b]* be in Ω*[v]*. Each has at least one pre-image in Ω*[p]*, *x[a]* and *x[b]* such that *p*(*x[a]*) = *z[a]* and *p*(*x[b]*) = *z[b]*, respectively, and by the path connectedness of Ω*[p]*, there is a path in Ω*[p]* from *x[a]* and *x[b]*. Applying *p* to this path yields a path in Ω*[v]* from *z[a]* and *z[b]*.

### **10.3 Multi-objective minimization**

Consider the *multi-objective minimization problem* (*MOMP*)

![image](images/eq10-12.jpg)

where *f* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^m*\[*x*\] is a vector of polynomial objectives,

![image](images/f0408-04.jpg)

*x* in ![image](images/ropf.jpg)*^n*, and the *feasible set* Ω*[p]* is the set given in (10.4). The entries of *f* are the *criteria* that measure the performances of the system and are possibly conflicting. The image through *f* of the set Ω*[p]* is called the *attainable set* and is defined as

![image](images/eq10-13.jpg)

When dealing with the MOMP (10.12), there need not be *x^◦* ∈ Ω*[p]* such that all criteria *f[i]*(*x*), *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, are simultaneously minimized at *x* = *x^◦*. To overcome this issue, the notion of the *Pareto*  *optimality* has been introduced to deal with multi-criteria optimization (see, e.g., Collette and Siarry, 2013).

**Definition 10.3.1.** A point *x^◦* ∈ Ω*[p]* is *Pareto optimal* for the MOMP (10.12) if there is no *x̂* ∈ Ω*[p]* such that *f[i]*(*x̂*) ![image](images/le.jpg)*f[i]*(*x^◦*) for all *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, and

![image](images/eq10-14.jpg)

for some *j* ∈ {1, . . . , *m*}.

Roughly speaking, a point *x^◦* is Pareto optimal for the MOMP (10.12) if there is no *x̂* ∈ Ω*[p]* that achieves an improved performance according to a criterion without degrading the performances of at least another criterion. Therefore, according to [Definition 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#def10-3-1), solving the MOMP (10.12) is equivalent to determine the set of all its Pareto optimal points. In the following, the set of all Pareto optimal points *x^◦* is denoted ![image](images/caps.jpg)⊆ Ω*[p]*, whereas the image through *f* of ![image](images/caps.jpg)(i.e., the set of the *Pareto optimal values*) is denoted ![image](images/capp.jpg)⊆ Ω*[v]*, ![image](images/capp.jpg)\= *f*(![image](images/caps.jpg)); for any *f^◦* ∈ ![image](images/capp.jpg), there is *x^◦* ∈ ![image](images/caps.jpg)such that *f*(*x^◦*) = *f^◦*.

The following theorem, used in [Algorithm 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#alg10-3-1), allows one to determine if *ẑ* ∈ Ω*[v]* is a Pareto optimal value.

**Theorem 10.3.1 (Contact Theorem, Lin, 1976).** *Let*

Three methods for the solution of the MOMP (10.12) are given. These methods rely on algebraic geometry and allow one to geometrically determine an expression of the Zariski closure of ![image](images/capp.jpg). The method in [Section 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3-1) is an algebraic variant of the weighted-sum-of-objective-functions method (see, e.g., Collette and Siarry, 2013, [Section 2.1](#chapter2.xhtml#sec2-1)); the technique given in [Section 10.3.2](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3-2) has some similarities with the hybrid method given in Collette and Siarry (2013, Section 2.5.2); the procedure given in [Section 10.3.3](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3-3) allows one to determine the envelope of a family of hyper–surfaces that contains the set ![image](images/capp.jpg). Unlike the techniques mentioned above, which are essentially based on numerical procedures, the methods given in this  chapter provide exact, closed-form solutions to the MOMP (10.12). Finally, an algorithm, which uses the Contact [Theorem 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#the10-3-1) to determine the points of this affine variety that are in ![image](images/capp.jpg)and the corresponding vectors in ![image](images/caps.jpg), is given in [Section 10.3.4](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3-4).

Since ![image](images/capp.jpg)⊆ ![image](images/capc.jpg)![image](images/capcstv.jpg), the following [Algorithm 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#alg10-3-1) (whose effectiveness is proved in [Theorem 10.3.7](#chapter10.xhtml#the10-3-7)) can be used to determine whether *ẑ* ∈ ![images](images/i0422-03.jpg)is in ![image](images/capp.jpg); such an algorithm uses a generalization of the numerical trick of [Lemma 10.2.5](#chapter10.xhtml#lem10-2-5) (Menini *et al*., 2018c).

Algorithm 10.3.1: Test for the Pareto optimality.

![image](images/alg10-3-1.jpg)

**Theorem 10.3.7.** *Let the MOMP* (10.12), *q*[1], . . . , *q[ℓ]* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)\[*z*\], *be such that* ![image](images/cappbar.jpg)⊆ **V**[![image](images/subropf.jpg)](*q*[1], . . . , *q[ℓ]*) = ![image](images/capc.jpg)![image](images/capcstv.jpg)*and z*^⋆ ∈ ![image](images/capc.jpg)![image](images/capcstv.jpg)*be given.* [*Algorithm* 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#alg10-3-1) *returns* true *if z*^⋆ ∈ ![image](images/capp.jpg)*or* false *if z*^⋆ ∉ ![image](images/capp.jpg).

**Proof.** [Algorithm 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#alg10-3-1) performs two tests. Firstly, at Steps 2–4, it checks if the point *z*^⋆ is in Ω*[v]*. Secondly, at Steps 7–17, it uses the Contact [Theorem 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#the10-3-1) to check if *z*^⋆ is a Pareto optimal value. Namely, at Steps 7–12, [Algorithm 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#alg10-3-1) determines if there is *x̂* ∈ Ω*[p]* that violates [Definition 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#def10-3-1), whereas at Steps 15–17, it uses Statement (10.2.5.4) of [Lemma 10.2.5](#chapter10.xhtml#lem10-2-5) to rule out the existence of an infimum. If these two conditions do not hold, then Ω*[v]∩*(*z*^⋆⊕![image](images/capc.jpg)) = {*z*^⋆} and, hence, by the Contact [Theorem 10.3.1](#chapter10.xhtml#the10-3-1), *z*^⋆ is in ![image](images/capp.jpg).

![image](images/squ.jpg)

The three methods presented in [Section 10.3](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-3) allow one to geometrically determine an affine variety that contains ![image](images/capp.jpg). ### **10.4 Solving control MOMPs**

To find a solution to Statements (10.1.1.a) and (10.1.1.b) of [Problem 10.1.1](#chapter10.xhtml#pro10-1-1), one needs a symbolic expression that relates the roots in *s* of *d*(*s, x*) and *x*. By the Abel–Ruffini Theorem, if the degree *μ* of *d*(*s, x*) in *s* is greater than 4, then there need not be a formula involving only radicals that relates the roots of *d* with the parameters *x*. The method presented in [Section 10.4.1](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10-4-1) is a variant of a method used in algebraic geometry for dealing with *symmetric*  *polynomials*, so to obtain implicit, but symbolic, expressions of the roots of a polynomial, being already in the Gröbner basis form.

## Chapter 11

## Distance to Internal Instability of Linear Time-Invariant Systems Under Structured Perturbations

### **11.1 Introduction**

The objective of this chapter is the study of the distance of linear time-invariant systems to internal instability (Menini *et al.*, 2020a). This study has a very long history in the literature (see, e.g., Loan, 1985; Gryazina *et al.*, 2008). A continuous-time linear time-invariant system

![image](images/f0439-01.jpg)

is exponentially stable if and only if all eigenvalues of its dynamic matrix *A* have negative real part. In many cases of theoretical and practical interest, only the nominal value *A^◦* ∈ ![image](images/ropf.jpg)^(*n*×*n*) of *A* is known, and the difference *δA* = *A*−*A^◦* represents *unstructured* perturbations from the nominal situation.

On the other hand, in several other cases (e.g., when dealing with mechanical and electrical systems in which the matrix entries are functions of some physical quantities), it is of interest to allow for *structured* perturbations of the nominal system, i.e., to let the entries of the matrix *A* vary in a structured way depending on a few uncertain parameters. In both cases, under the assumption that the nominal system is exponentially stable, it is important to know how large the perturbations may be still preserving the exponential stability of the perturbed system.

The aim of this chapter is to extend the analysis already available in the unstructured case (that is briefly reviewed in [Section 11.2](#chapter11.xhtml#sec11-2)) to the structured one, allowing the parameters to affect the system in a polynomial way. The main aspects of the chapter can be summarized as follows:

(i) Both continuous-time and discrete-time linear time-invariant systems are considered.

(ii) The uncertain parameters affect the system equations in a polynomial way, 

![image](images/f0440-01.jpg)

where Δ is either the time derivative (in the continuous-time case) or the one-step forward shift operator (in the discretetime case), and the entries of *E*(*β*), *A*(*β*) are polynomial functions of a vector *β* of parameters.

(iii) If the system is well connected (Doyle *et al.*, 2013) (i.e., det(*E*(*β*)) ≠ 0), then 

![image](images/f0440-02.jpg)

thus including the case of the unknown parameters affecting the system in a rational way.

(iv) The unstructured case can be included in the analysis as a sub-case letting the entries of *E* − *E^◦* and *A* − *A^◦* (where ^◦ denotes the nominal case) be the uncertain parameters.

(v) General distance functions in the parameter space can be adopted, including the Euclidean distance.

(vi) The internal exponential stability (i.e., well-posedness and exponential stability) is considered.

(vii) The problem of computing the distance of a nominal system to internal instability is reformulated as the problem of computing the distance of a point to an affine variety.

(viii) A method is given to compute the distance of the nominal system to internal instability.

(ix) Two methods are given for choosing the nominal system in the center (both analytic and Chebyshev centers are considered) of one of the possible compact connected components of the  domain of stability, so that the nominal system is sufficiently far from instability. Note that choosing the system model as *E*(*β*) Δ*x*(*t*) = *A*(*β*) *x*(*t*) allows one to tackle both differential-algebraic systems and the cases when the loss of well-posedness is due to the interconnection of internal sub-systems (Doyle *et al.*, 2013).

Therefore, the techniques proposed in this chapter can be used to study the distance to internal instability of differential-algebraic, linear, time-invariant systems whose dynamic matrices depend on some parameters, either in a polynomial or rational way.

Several other types of metrics have been used in the literature to measure the distance between two systems, such as the gap (Georgiou and Smith, 1990), the graph (Vidyasagar, 1984), and the *ν*\-gap metrics (Vinnicombe, 1993). Unlike these metrics, which account for the distance between the transfer functions of the nominal and the perturbed systems, the squared distance functions considered here (see [Definition 11.4.1](#chapter11.xhtml#def11-4-1)) account for the distance between the nominal and the perturbed values of the system parameters, so that the measure of robustness is based on quantities that have a direct physical meaning (possibly suitably weighted).

If only *real* unstructured perturbations *δA* are allowed, then the *real unstructured distance to instability* is measured through the *real radius of stability*, which is given by (Qiu *et al.*, 1995)

In particular, if

Let

if a static output feedback *u*(*t*) = *K y*(*t*) is considered, the closed-loop system is given by

![image](images/f0442-05.jpg)

Hence, although the parameters linearly affect the perturbation *δA* = *B^◦ K C^◦*, the important case of closed-loop systems under uncertain static output feedback is covered by the uncertainty *δA* = *B^◦ K C^◦*. Clearly, the linearity of the perturbation yielded the above nice results.

With any perturbation *δA*, one can associate the number *N*(*δA*) of eigenvalues of *A* = *A^◦* + *δA* having negative real part; clearly, *N*(*δA*) ∈ {0, 1, . . . , *n*}, and the exponential stability of the system corresponds to *N*(*δA*) = *n*: the domain of stability is the set of all perturbations *δA* for which *N*(*δA*) = *n*. The number *N*(*δA*) can only change in correspondence of the perturbations for which the roots of the characteristic polynomial of *A* have zero real part. The set of all these points is called the boundary of the D-decomposition of the uncertain parameter space. The boundary of the domain of stability is a subset of the boundary of the D-decomposition (Gryazina and Polyak, 2006; Gryazina *et al.*, 2008).

Now, if *d*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, *β*) is separating for **V**[![image](images/subcopf.jpg)](![image](images/capk1.jpg)) and the reduced Gröbner basis of ![image](images/capk1.jpg), with respect to the Lex monomial order, with Λ[1] ≻[Lex] . . . ≻[Lex] Λ*[r]* ≻[Lex] *β*[1] ≻[Lex] . . . ≻[Lex] *β[m]* ≻[Lex] *τ*, is in the Shape Lemma form (11.23), then to each real root of *Q* there corresponds a real critical point; hence, the smallest real root of *Q* cannot be negative, because in that case two non-real critical points would be mapped by *d*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, *β*) into the same root of *Q*, but this cannot happen because *d*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*^◦, *β*) is separating.

Following Luenberger *et al.* (1984) and Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004), two alternatives for “farthest” are considered: the *analytic centers* and the *Chebyshev centers*.

**Theorem 11.7.2.** *Let* ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i] be one of the connected component of* ![image](images/caps.jpg)*;* *if* ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i] is non-empty and* ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]* ∪ *∂*![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i] is compact, then there is an analytic center ![image](images/alphacirc.jpg)[c] in* ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i].*

Since ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]* is non-empty and ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]* ∪ *∂*![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]* is compact, the continuous function *h[p]*(*β*) takes a maximum value on ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]* ∪ *∂*![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]*; such a maximum value must necessarily be positive. This implies that the maximum value of *h[p]* is not attained on the boundary *∂*![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]*, since *h[p]*(*![image](images/betacirc.jpg)*) = 0 along *∂*![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]*, and, hence, it is attained on an interior point of ![image](images/caps.jpg)*[i]*.

For the case (iii), the reader is referred to Rudin (2000).

For showing that ![image](images/i0502-01.jpg)explicit examples in ![image](images/i0502-02.jpg)were given in Motzkin (1967); Robinson (1969); Choi and Lam (1977); Reznick (1978):

![image](images/f0502-05.jpg)

Hilbert posed a generalization of his results as the 17th Problem: “must any PSD form *p* be an SOS of rational functions?” A positive  answer was given in Artin (1927) in a rather abstract way. Pólya (1928) gave an explicit solution to the Hilbert 17th Problem for “even” PD forms, using a result that is now known as the Pólya Theorem (Hardy *et al.*, 1952). Later, the Pólya Theorem was used to directly prove that a (not necessarily even) PD form is an SOS of rational functions (Habicht, 1939). Note that, when dealing with polynomials, there is no loss of generality in considering, as in this chapter, only forms, because the properties of being PSD and SOS are transferred upon de-homogenization and preserved upon homogenization. Nevertheless, the property of being PD is not preserved upon homogenization. Due to the above cases, one might guess that “most” PSD forms are SOS, but Blekherman (2006) showed that, for sufficiently high values of *d*, there exist more PSD forms than SOS’s and that the “difference” between ![image](images/i0503-01.jpg)grows as the number of variables increases.

The *Gram matrix method* (Choi *et al.*, 1995), which originated from the *term-inspection method* (Reznick, 1978), is one of the fundamental steps that allows the automatic construction of SOS’s. The Gram matrix method consists in the observation that if a form *p* of total degree 2*d* can be represented as an SOS,

![image](images/f0503-01.jpg)

with the *h[i]*’s being forms of total degree *d*, one can associate with such an SOS a matrix *Q*, called the *Gram matrix*, which depends on the coefficients of the forms *h[i]*. Hence, by considering all possible expressions of *p* as SOS and the corresponding Gram matrices, one obtains a set ![image](images/i0504-01.jpg)of Gram matrices associated with *p*. If *p* is an SOS, then *m* is the minimum integer such that ![image](images/i0504-02.jpg)for some forms *h[i]*’s, if and only if *m* is the minimum rank of *Q*, as *Q* varies in ![image](images/i0504-03.jpg)such an *m* is called the *length* of *p*. Semi-algebraic sets can precisely be characterized by means of quantifier elimination and cylindrical algebraic decomposition (Collins, 1975), which, however, present an inherent high complexity. Another fundamental step for obtaining an efficient procedure for the computation of an SOS is realizing that ![image](images/capl.jpg)is convex (Nesterov, 2000; Parrilo, 2000) and that there is a strong relationship between convex optimization problems (semi-definite Programs) and SOS decompositions; it is worth pointing out that SPD methods also make it possible to optimize over SOS polynomials. Since convex optimization problems can efficiently be solved by interior point methods (Vandenberghe and Boyd, 1996), the computation of an SOS decomposition of a form is now tractable. There exist several efficient solvers (e.g., `SeDuMi`, see Sturm, 1999) of convex optimization problems and two `MATLAB` toolboxes that are widely used for their modeling and solution, `SOSTOOLS` (Papachristodoulou *et al.*, 2013) and `YALMIP` (Löfberg, 2009), by interfacing with external solvers. Thanks to such toolboxes, various techniques based on SOS decompositions are nowadays used in many applications of systems and control theory (Prajna *et al.*, 2004; Raman *et al.*, 2016).

Typically, the output of the algorithms described above is numerically approximated, and this may be a problem in some cases. One possibility to obtain an exact *weighted SOS* (wSOS) with positive weights (wSOS^+) decomposition, over the field ![image](images/qopf.jpg)of rational numbers, is proposed in Peyrl and Parrilo (2008, 2007) (see, also, Kaltofen *et al.*, 2012; Powers, 2011), where, under a strict feasibility assumption, it is shown that an approximate solution of the semi-definite program is sufficient to obtain a rational wSOS^+ decomposition of  the given polynomial. Qualitatively, the strict feasibility assumption consists in assuming that there are interior points of ![image](images/capl.jpg)sufficiently far from the boundary of ![image](images/capl.jpg). Recently, it has been shown (see Henrion *et al.*, 2016) that LMI feasibility problems can be solved without a strict feasibility assumption. If *p* can be rewritten as a wSOS with *m*^∗ squares, but not less, then *m*^∗ is called the *w-length* of *p* (Menini *et al.*, 2018a).

The idea pursued in this chapter is to construct wSOS^+ decompositions without passing through numerically approximated computations, working in some field ![image](images/kopf.jpg)containing the rationals and contained in the reals. When moving from ![image](images/ropf.jpg)to such a ![image](images/kopf.jpg), the complexity of the problem increases, e.g., one important question is: “if *p* is a polynomial with coefficients in ![image](images/qopf.jpg)that is SOS over ![image](images/kopf.jpg)(possibly, ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\= ![image](images/ropf.jpg)), then is *p* also a sum of squares over ![image](images/qopf.jpg)?” If ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is a totally real field, Galois over ![image](images/qopf.jpg), Hillar (2009) showed that the answer is positive, whereas the answer is negative if ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\= ![image](images/ropf.jpg), as shown in Scheiderer (2012), where it is proved that the form

![image](images/f0507-01.jpg)

is a sum of two squares over the reals (actually, over a totally real field, not Galois over ![image](images/qopf.jpg)), but it is not a sum of any number of squares over the rationals; this is just one of the difficulties that arise when moving from ![image](images/ropf.jpg)to ![image](images/qopf.jpg). A complete answer to the above question has been given in the case of forms with *n* = 2 (i.e., upon de-homogenization, for univariate polynomials with rational coefficients); Landau (1906) showed that any PSD form of two variables, with rational coefficients, can always be written as a sum of 8 squares over the rationals, and such a result was improved by Pourchet (1971), who demonstrated that 5 squares are sufficient. Some algorithms for the computation of SOS decompositions of bivariate forms over the rationals can be found in Menini and Tornambe (2015).

(ii) If either *p* or −*p* is PSD, then [Algorithm 12.2.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-2-1) returns a wSOS decomposition of *p*, with the weights having the same sign.

(iii) If both *p* and −*p* are not PSD, then [Algorithm 12.2.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-2-1) terminates with a wSOS decomposition where the weights have different signs.

(iv) [Algorithm 12.2.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-2-1) can be applied also when ![image](images/kopf.jpg)is a finite algebraic extension of ![image](images/qopf.jpg).

However, the method given in [Section 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-3) can be applied, as a certificate of positive (semi-)definiteness, without the restriction *n* > *m*.

### **12.6 Randomly generated experiments**

Randomly generated experiments have been carried out to compare either [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) in the case *n* > *m* or the procedure presented in [Section 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-3) in the case *n* ![image](images/ge.jpg)*m*, both implemented in `Macaulay2` (Grayson and Stillman, 2020), with the `MATLAB` toolboxes `SOSTOOLS` (Papachristodoulou *et al.*, 2013) and `YALMIP` (Löfberg, 2009), interfaced with the solver `SeDuMi` (Sturm, 1999). All experiments have been carried out on a laptop running Windows 8.1, with an Intel Core i5 3210M CPU (2.50 GHz) processor and 6 GB of RAM DDR3. In each experiment, the weights *w[i]* and the coefficients of the forms *h[i]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\]*[d]*, *i* = 1, . . . , *m*, have been generated as random integers uniformly distributed in the intervals \[1, 100\] and \[−100, 100\], respectively, and the corresponding form *p* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)\[*x*\][\=2*d*] has been obtained by substituting such values in ![image](images/i0547-02.jpg)For 2*d* = 4, *n* varies in {2, . . . , 6} and *m* varies in {1, . . . , 4}, for a total of 20 tests, whose results are reported in [Table 12.2](#chapter12.xhtml#tab12-2); for 2*d* = 6, *n* varies in {2, . . . , 5} and *m* varies in {1, 2, 3}, for a total of 12 tests, whose results are reported in [Table 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#tab12-3); for 2*d* = 8, *n* varies in {2, 3, 4} and *m* varies in {1, 2, 3}, for a total of 9 tests, whose results are reported in [Table 12.4](#chapter12.xhtml#tab12-4). In each test, the same set of 1000 forms (100 forms only for the more complex test 2*d* = 8, *n* = 4, *m* = 3), randomly generated as above, has been used as input to

Table 12.2: Results of the randomly generated experiments: Case 2*d* = 4.

![image](images/tab12-2.jpg)

(a) either [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) in the case *n* > *m* or the procedure presented in [Section 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-3) in the case *n* ![image](images/le.jpg)*m*, and in this last case the results are reported in boldface (sub-table referred to as Alg. Geom.),

(b) the `MATLAB` toolbox `SOSTOOLS`, with the solver `SeDuMi`, using the function `findsos` with the `rational` flag (sub-table referred to as `SOSTOOLS` rational),

(c) the `MATLAB` toolbox `SOSTOOLS`, with the solver `SeDuMi`, using the function `findsos` without the `rational` flag (sub-table referred to as `SOSTOOLS` numeric),

(d) the `MATLAB` toolbox `YALMIP`, with the solver `SeDuMi`, using the functions `sos` and `solvesos` (sub-table referred to as `YALMIP` numeric).

Table 12.3: Results of the randomly generated experiments: Case 2*d* = 6.

More than 40.000 different forms have been considered. Each table corresponds to the same value of 2*d*, and the entries of the subtables (a), (b), (c) and (d) (corresponding to the same pair *m, n*) are referred to the same test. Each entry of the sub-tables reports two numbers: the average execution time ![image](images/tb.jpg)(either with a wSOS^+ decomposition or with a failure) and the % of exact rational wSOS^+ decompositions obtained when Alg. Geom. or `SOSTOOLS` rational are used, and the percentage of approximated wSOS^+ decompositions obtained without running into numerical errors, when `SOSTOOLS` numeric or `YALMIP` numeric are used.

Table 12.4: Results of the randomly generated experiments: Case 2*d* = 8.

The procedures proposed in this chapter (case (a) in the tables) give an exact certificate of the forms being PSD in 100% of the cases, with different execution times depending on the complexity of the analyzed form. If 2*d* = 4, [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) produces an exact rational wSOS^+ with ![image](images/tb.jpg)ranging from 0.16ms (when *n* = 2, *m* = 1) to 15.33s (when *n* = 6, *m* = 4), whereas the procedure presented in [Section 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-3) produces an exact certificate of being PSD with ![image](images/tb.jpg)ranging from 2, 61ms (when *n* = 2, *m* = 2) to 47.16s (when *n* = 4, *m* = 4). Similar results are obtained for 2*d* = 6 and 2*d* = 8, with the worst average execution time obtained with [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) when 2*d* = 8, *n* = 4, *m* = 3, with ![image](images/tb.jpg)\= 2.04hours. In this case, the considered 100 forms *p* are constituted each by 165 monomials of total degree 8, and the three forms *h*[1], *h*[2], *h*[3] have 35 monomials, with a total of 108 coefficients (including the weights) to be determined. For the test 2*d* = 8, *n* = 4, *m* = 3, `SOSTOOLS` rational gives an exact rational wSOS^+ in 6% of the cases, `SOSTOOLS` numeric gives an approximate wSOS^+, without running into numerical errors, in 8% of the cases, and `YALMIP` numeric gives an approximate wSOS^+, without running into numerical errors, in 4% of the cases. `SOSTOOLS` rational, `SOSTOOLS` numeric and `YALMIP` numeric work very well when *n* ![image](images/ge.jpg)*m*: they give exact rational wSOS^+’s, and approximate wSOS^+’s without running into numerical errors, in 100% of the cases, with a maximum average execution time of 0.83s; in addition, such average execution times are often lower than the corresponding times when the procedure presented in [Section 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-3) is used. Contrarily, `SOSTOOLS` rational, `SOSTOOLS` numeric and `YALMIP` numeric do not work well when *n* > *m*, and in particular in many cases no exact rational wSOS^+, and no approximate wSOS^+ without running into numerical errors, is obtained. From these results, it can be concluded that [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) is complementary to the two `MATLAB` toolboxes `SOSTOOLS` and `YALMIP`, with the solver `SeDuMi`.

### **12.8 wSOS^+ decomposition through tools of linear algebra**

The main objective of this section is to provide a technique based on linear algebra to find, if any, a wSOS^+ decomposition of a given form of total degree 2*d* whose length *m* is lower than the number *n* of variables (Menini *et al.*, 2019d). To reach such a result, in [Section 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-1) a procedure is given to compute the Gröbner basis up to total degree *d* of the saturation of the gradient ideal by a variable through the reduced row echelon form. Similar results are used in [Section 12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-2) to determine a polynomial representation of a form of total degree 2*d* in terms of forms of total degree *d*. In [Section 12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-3), a linear algebra tool to perform the “completing the square” procedure is proposed. Finally, in [Section 12.8.4](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-4) these three techniques are combined to outline a procedure able to find, if any, a wSOS^+ decomposition of a “generic” form of total degree 2*d* in the case *n* > *m*. Examples are reported to illustrate the proposed methods.

#### **12.8.3 *Linear algebra implementation of the “completing the square” procedure***

In this section, a linear algebra technique, which provides the same results of the “completing the square” procedure to be executed at Step 9 of [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1), is given. Unlike the procedure given in Rajwade (1993, Theorem 6.1), such a technique is guaranteed to provide a wSOS decomposition of the input form only if it can be represented as a wSOS^+, whereas it may fail if the input form *p* is not sign definite. Such a limitation of the proposed method is not an issue in practical applications, where the attention is focused just on wSOS^+ (see, for instance, Prajna *et al.*, 2004, 2007; Papachristodoulou and Prajna, 2002, 2005; Chesi, 2010; Ahmadi *et al.*, 2014; Raman *et al.*, 2016).

Consider the following technical lemma.

**Lemma 12.8.1.** *Let p*(*x*) = *z*^⊤(*x*)*Az*(*x*), *where z*(*x*) = *Jx, J* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*n*), *and A* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*)*. Without loss of generality, assume that n* ![image](images/ge.jpg)*m, that J is in the reduced row echelon form, that it has full rowrank, and that A is symmetric and invertible. Hence,* ![image](images/i0568-01.jpg)*is the reduced row echelon form of ![image](images/i0568-02.jpg)from which the zero rows have been removed.*

Let *H* be the Hessian matrix of the quadratic form *p* and let *J* = ![image](images/cape.jpg)*[r]*(*H*) be its row reduced echelon form from which the zero rows have been removed. Using the relation given in (12.8), one has that the matrix

Since such a matrix need not be diagonal (and, hence, the obtained expression need not be a wSOS), consider the following lemma that proposes a factorization of the matrix *A* as the product of triangular matrices times a diagonal one.

**Lemma 12.8.2 (Cholesky Factorization, Meyer, 2000).** *Let A* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg)^(*m*×*m*) *be a positive definite, symmetric matrix. Thus, A can uniquely be decomposed into a product of the following form* (*called* LDLT decomposition of A):

Note that an LDLT decomposition of non-definite matrices can successfully be computed even if the matrix *A* depends on some symbolic parameters. Combining the results given in [Lemmas 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#lem12-8-1) and [12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#lem12-8-2), the following [Algorithm 12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-3) allows one to find, if any, a wSOS^+ decomposition of a given quadratic form.

Algorithm 12.8.3: The “completing the square” procedure through linear algebra.

![image](images/alg12-8-3.jpg)

Note that also Step 4 of [Algorithm 12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-3) can easily be carried out through linear algebra techniques. As a matter of fact, to determine if *A* is positive definite, it is sufficient to compute all of its leading minors. If all such determinants are positive, then *A* is positive definite, otherwise it is not (Possieri and Sassano, 2015).

**Remark 12.8.2.** It is worth noting that, in principle, a wSOS decomposition of the quadratic form *p* can directly be obtained computing an LDLT decomposition of the Hessian matrix *H*. However, since numerical algorithms to compute LDLT decomposition perform better if the input matrix is non-singular, it has been preferred, in [Algorithm 12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-3), to compute the LDLT decomposition of the matrix *A* (that, by [Lemma 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#lem12-8-1), is non-singular) rather than the one of *H* directly.

#### **12.8.4 *wSOS*^+ *representation***

In this section, the procedures given in [Sections 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-1), [12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-2), and [12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12-8-3) are combined to provide a procedure able to “generically” find a wSOS^+ decomposition of a form that can be represented as the weighted sum of *m* < *n* squares with positive weights.

By [Theorem 12.4.3](#chapter12.xhtml#the12-4-3), if the form *p* can be represented as *p* = ![image](images/i0571-01.jpg)for some forms *h*[1], . . . , *h[m]* of total degree *d* and for some *w*[1], . . . , *w[m]* ∈ ![image](images/kopf.jpg), with *m* > *n*, then [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) “generically” returns a wSOS representation of *p*. By [Fact 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#fac12-8-1), [Algorithm 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-1) allows one to carry out Step 1 of [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) of such a procedure, by [Fact 12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#fac12-8-2), [Algorithm 12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-2) allows one to execute Step 7 of [Algorithm 12.4.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-4-1) and, by [Lemmas 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#lem12-8-1) and [12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#lem12-8-2), [Algorithm 12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-3) allows one to perform the “completing the square” procedure. Therefore, the following [Algorithm 12.8.4](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-4) (which combines [Algorithms 12.8.1](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-1), [12.8.2](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-2), and [12.8.3](#chapter12.xhtml#alg12-8-3)) allows one to find, if any, a wSOS^+ decomposition of a given form.
